issues.name: Housing supply & zoning preemption
issues.short_description: How hard should the state push cities to build more housing — even when local residents object?
issues.ca_specific_context: Local control under CEQA and city zoning has historically blocked dense infill; recent state law (SB 9, SB 10, SB 423) preempts some of that.

stance_scale.label: Push hard — override local zoning rules to force more building
Push a lot — set strong building targets, override cities somewhat
Strike a balance — encourage building but leave most decisions to cities
Mostly leave it to cities — limit state override, cut local red tape instead
Focus on subsidized housing and renter protections rather than forcing market-rate building

voter_guide.current_policy: Over the past decade, California has taken a lot of power over housing approvals away from cities and given it to the state. [SB 35](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB35) (2017) created a fast track for qualifying apartment projects in cities that miss their state housing targets: approval becomes "ministerial," meaning local officials must say yes if the rules are met, with no discretion to say no. [SB 423](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB423) (2023) extended that fast track to 2036 and stretched it into parts of the coast. [SB 9](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB9) (2021) made it possible to build duplexes and split lots on most single-family properties "by right" — meaning approval is automatic if you meet the rules. The state also gives each region a housing target, called a Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA). When a city's local housing plan is out of step with the law, a state rule called the Housing Accountability Act limits its power to reject housing — and [AB 1893](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB1893) (2024) put real teeth into the "Builder's Remedy," which lets developers bypass local zoning in cities that aren't meeting their housing goals.
key_facts: The current RHNA cycle (2023–2031) calls for about 2.5 million new homes statewide — roughly 1 million of them affordable to lower-income families.

[SB 9](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB9) (2021) was used far less than expected. In its first year, Los Angeles got 211 unit applications, San Francisco 25, San Diego 7, and San José just 1 — even though a 2021 Terner Center analysis had estimated about 700,000 units could become newly feasible.
Cities that don't comply with state housing-plan law can be fined $10,000 to $600,000 a month.

The [SB 35](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB35) / [SB 423](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB423) fast track only kicks in where a city is missing its housing targets or doesn't have a state-approved housing plan. SB 423 also added wage and skilled-worker requirements that scale with project size.
The Surplus Land Act requires local agencies to give affordable housing first priority when they sell off public land they no longer need.
voter_guide.comparison: California has gone further than almost any state in overriding local zoning. A few others have moved this way too — Oregon ended single-family-only zoning statewide in 2019, and Montana and Washington passed broad laws in 2023 allowing more housing on existing lots. But many states still leave land-use decisions almost entirely to cities and towns.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: Supporters of stronger state control say local government caused a housing shortage that has lasted decades. The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) traces the state's nation-leading rents and home prices directly to building too little near coastal job centers. Supporters argue cities cave to homeowner pressure to block new housing, so only firm state mandates — automatic "by-right" approval, enforceable targets, and the Builder's Remedy — can close the gap. They point to [SB 9](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB9) as proof that voluntary tools fall flat when cities still have room to drag their feet.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: Opponents say land-use decisions belong with local officials, who know their own neighborhoods — the roads, the fire risk, the traffic, the character of the place. They argue statewide, one-size-fits-all mandates override plans that local voters approved, and that fast-tracked "by-right" projects can skip environmental review and public input. They also say the real causes of the shortage are high construction costs, interest rates, and a tight labor supply — not zoning — so overriding cities adds conflict without reliably producing affordable homes.
voter_guide.note_on_options: This is a single axis measuring how hard the state should push to expand market-rate housing supply — from aggressively preempting local zoning (option 1) down to prioritizing subsidies and tenant protections over state-forced supply (option 5). Candidates can reach the low end for different reasons: some defend local control and single-family neighborhoods (option 4), while others favor public/subsidized housing over market-rate construction (option 5). A position here signals how much the candidate would use state power to override local zoning for supply.

issues.name: Homelessness response
issues.short_description: How should California handle homelessness — lean more on enforcement, or on housing and services?
issues.ca_specific_context: Prop 1 (2024) expanded conservatorship and mental-health funding; cities differ widely on encampment sweeps; SB 43 widened the bar for conservatorship.

stance_scale.label: Clear encampments and expand court-ordered treatment as the main tools
Lead with enforcement, but offer services at the same time
Balance the two — only clear camps when shelter or services are available
Lead with housing first; use enforcement sparingly
Invest heavily in housing and services; use enforcement only as a last resort

voter_guide.current_policy: California's official rule is "Housing First": state-funded programs are supposed to offer people permanent housing right away, without first requiring them to get sober or accept treatment. This is written into state law (Welfare & Institutions Code §8255). On top of that, the state has recently added enforcement and treatment options. The CARE Act ([SB 1338](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB1338), passed in 2022) set up civil courts that can order a treatment plan for people with untreated schizophrenia-type disorders, and every county was running it by December 2024. [Proposition 1](https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2024/prop-1-mental-health/) (March 2024) approved a $6.4 billion bond for mental-health housing and treatment and shifted some existing mental-health funds. After the U.S. Supreme Court's [Grants Pass v. Johnson](https://calmatters.org/housing/2024/06/california-homeless-camps-grants-pass-ruling/) ruling (June 2024), Governor Newsom told state agencies and cities to clear encampments and shared a model anti-camping ordinance they could adopt.
key_facts: 187,084 Californians were counted as homeless in the January 2024 one-night count, up 3.1% from 181,399 the year before (HUD).
California has roughly 25% of the nation's homeless population and the highest share living outside — about two-thirds sleep on the street rather than in shelters.

[Grants Pass v. Johnson](https://calmatters.org/housing/2024/06/california-homeless-camps-grants-pass-ruling/) (Supreme Court, 6-3, June 2024) ruled that banning public camping does not violate the Eighth Amendment. That removed the earlier legal barrier to ticketing or arresting people for camping even when no shelter is available.

[Proposition 1](https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2024/prop-1-mental-health/) (2024) approved $6.4 billion for mental-health housing and treatment, including about $4.4 billion to build roughly 10,000 treatment beds.

By early 2026, more than 3,800 CARE Act petitions had been filed since the program went statewide in December 2024, and the state added $291 million in March 2026 for CARE-related services and housing.
voter_guide.comparison: California's homeless population grew about 3% in 2024 — much smaller than the roughly 18% jump in homelessness nationwide. But the state still has the most homeless people of any state, the largest share of the country's total, and the highest portion sleeping outside. Most other big states get a far larger share of their homeless residents into shelters.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who favor a services-led, Housing First approach (the high end of the scale) say a stable home is what makes it possible to tackle addiction and mental illness — not a reward you earn afterward. They point to studies showing Housing First keeps people housed. They argue that clearing camps just moves people around without shrinking the population, and saddles them with criminal records that make it even harder to find housing. And they warn that expanding forced treatment or conservatorship risks coercing people who were never offered enough voluntary help first.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who favor more enforcement, treatment mandates, and conservatorship (the low end) say California has spent over $20 billion on homelessness in recent years while the share living outside stayed near the highest in the country. They argue that housing alone doesn't work for the many people on the street with untreated serious mental illness or addiction, that visible encampments create real health and safety problems, and that the Grants Pass ruling now lets the state pair an offer of shelter and treatment with consequences if someone refuses.
voter_guide.note_on_options: This scale runs from enforcement-and-mandated-treatment (1) to pure Housing First with no enforcement (5). Many candidates favor combinations — e.g., expanded treatment beds plus voluntary housing — that fall in the middle; the endpoints represent the contested questions of whether to condition housing on treatment and whether to use camping-ban enforcement.

voter_guide.explainer: "Housing First" means giving someone a permanent place to live right away, without first requiring them to get sober or accept treatment — the idea is that it's easier to deal with addiction or mental illness once you have a roof over your head. A "conservatorship" is a court order that puts another person or agency in charge of decisions for someone a judge finds unable to care for themselves. "CARE Court" is a newer civil court track that can order a treatment plan for people with serious untreated mental illness. The "point-in-time count" (PIT count) is a one-night tally each January of how many people are homeless.

issues.name: Top-bracket and corporate tax rates
issues.short_description: Should CA raise or cut income and corporate tax rates on top earners and businesses?
issues.ca_specific_context: Top marginal personal income rate is 13.3% (highest in the US); the corporate rate is 8.84%.

stance_scale.label: Cut top-bracket and corporate rates
Hold current rates
Modestly raise top-bracket and/or corporate rates
Substantially raise top-bracket and corporate rates
Substantially raise rates and add new higher brackets

voter_guide.current_policy: California's top personal income tax rate is 13.3% — the highest of any state. It applies to taxable income above roughly $1 million, and voters made it permanent through [Prop 30](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=30&year=2012) (2012) and [Prop 55](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016) (2016). On top of that, a 1% Mental Health Services Tax from [Prop 63](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=63&year=2004) (2004) applies to income over $1 million, and a 2024 change added another 1.1% on wages over $1 million to fund state disability insurance. The tax on company profits has been 8.84% (10.84% for banks) since 1997.
key_facts: Top individual rate: 13.3% — the highest in the U.S. Next closest: New York 10.9%, New Jersey 10.75%, Oregon 9.9%.
The top 1% of filers pay roughly half of all personal income tax the state collects (Legislative Analyst's Office).
The 8.84% tax on company profits is middle-of-the-pack among states that tax corporate income.
Texas, Florida, Nevada, Washington, and several other states have no state income tax at all.
Leaning so heavily on top earners makes the state's revenue progressive but unstable — it swings sharply up in good years and down in recessions.
voter_guide.comparison: California's tax system is more progressive than most states', leaning hard on top earners — but that also makes its revenue more volatile. Add in federal taxes, and the highest earners face a combined top rate above 50%.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: Supporters of raising rates on top earners or companies say the wealthiest residents and most profitable corporations captured most of the state's income growth, so they can afford to pay more. They argue steady revenue is needed to avoid cutting safety-net programs, and that California can ask more of its top earners without scaring off the income they generate.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: Opponents say California already has the nation's highest top rates. They point to IRS data showing more high-income filers have moved out to no-tax states than have moved in since 2020, argue that depending on a small group of top earners makes the budget wildly unpredictable, and warn that higher taxes on company profits push more headquarters to leave the state.

issues.name: State wealth tax
issues.short_description: Should California tax the net worth of its very richest residents — a tax on wealth itself, separate from income tax?
issues.ca_specific_context: Two distinct proposals: AB 259 (2023, Asm. Alex Lee) sought an annual tax on net worth over $50M but stalled in committee; the One-Time Wealth Tax / 'Billionaire Tax Act' (SEIU-UHW) qualified for the November 2026 ballot as a one-time 5% tax on billionaires. Neither is law.

stance_scale.label: Oppose a state wealth tax
Lean against it — no current support
Open to it / undecided
Support a wealth tax
Strongly support a wealth tax on the ultra-rich

voter_guide.current_policy: California has no wealth tax — a tax on what someone owns (their net worth) rather than the income they earn. Two different versions have been floated, and they work very differently. In 2023, Asm. Alex Lee's [AB 259](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB259) (with constitutional amendment ACA 3) proposed an annual tax — 1% on net worth above $50 million and 1.5% above $1 billion — but it stalled in committee and never became law. Separately, a one-time measure — the 'Billionaire Tax Act,' formally the One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative, backed by SEIU-UHW — qualified for the November 2026 ballot: a single 5% tax on the net worth of California billionaires, with revenue going mostly to health care and the rest to education and food assistance.
key_facts: No U.S. state currently has a true wealth tax.

These are two different proposals. [AB 259](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB259) (2023, Alex Lee) was an annual tax — 1% on net worth over $50 million, 1.5% over $1 billion — that stalled in committee and never became law.

The measure on the November 2026 ballot is a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of California billionaires (over $1 billion), assessed as of a set date — not a recurring tax. Most of the revenue is earmarked for health care, with a share for education and food assistance.
A one-time tax is owed once, on wealth as of a snapshot date; an annual tax recurs every year the wealth is held. The 2023 bill was annual; the 2026 ballot measure is one-time.

Broad wealth taxes have been proposed and failed in Washington, New York, Massachusetts, and Illinois. The hardest part of any wealth tax is valuing things without a clear market price — private companies, art, real estate.
voter_guide.comparison: California would be the first U.S. state to run a true tax on total wealth. Several other high-tax states looked at the idea and passed on it, citing legal challenges, the difficulty of valuing assets, and the risk that the wealthiest residents simply move away.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: Supporters say a wealth tax reaches fortunes that income taxes miss — billionaires can keep their taxable income low while their net worth keeps growing — and that even a modest tax on the very largest fortunes could fund schools, health care, and child care from a narrow group of taxpayers.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: Opponents say a state wealth tax runs into serious legal and practical problems (how do you value someone's assets?), that the most mobile residents would leave or restructure to avoid it, and that revenue resting on a handful of people would be unpredictable.

voter_guide.current_policy: Under [Prop 13](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3497) (1978), all California property — homes, stores, offices, and factories — is taxed at 1% of its purchase price, and the taxable value can rise no more than 2% a year until the property is sold and reassessed. Business property gets no separate ("split-roll") treatment. [Prop 15](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=15&year=2020) (2020) would have changed that for most commercial and industrial property, taxing it at current market value while leaving homes under Prop 13's rules. It failed, 52% to 48%.
key_facts: [Prop 13](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3497) caps the property tax rate at 1% of the purchase price and limits annual growth in taxable value to 2% — until the property changes hands and is reassessed.

The LAO estimated [Prop 15](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=15&year=2020) would have raised $6.5 billion to $11.5 billion a year for local governments and schools once fully phased in (around 2025).
Of that money, roughly 60% would have gone to cities, counties, and special districts, and 40% to schools and community colleges (LAO).
Prop 15 left homes out entirely. It also exempted small businesses with $3 million or less in California commercial property, plus up to $500,000 of business equipment.
Prop 15 lost statewide, 51.9% to 48.1%, in November 2020.
voter_guide.comparison: California is unusual in taxing business and residential property the same way — locking both to the purchase price. Most states reassess all property toward current market value every so often. As a result, a California commercial building held for decades can be taxed far below a nearly identical one that sold recently.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: Supporters of a commercial split-roll say [Prop 13](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3497)'s purchase-price rule lets long-held business property — office towers, malls, big industrial sites — be taxed on values that are decades out of date. That shifts more of the tax load onto newer owners and homeowners. They point to the LAO's $6.5–$11.5 billion estimate as steady money for schools and local services, and argue that taxing business property at market value — while still protecting homeowners and small businesses — fixes the imbalance without touching home protections.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: Opponents say higher taxes on commercial property get passed down to tenants — small businesses, restaurants, renters — and ultimately to shoppers, raising prices across the economy. They warn that reassessing property at market value every year is complicated and invites lawsuits, that it would hit businesses hardest in downturns when values and rents are shaky, and that weakening Prop 13 for any kind of property opens the door to chipping away at home protections later — undoing the predictability voters voted for in 1978.
voter_guide.note_on_options: The scale is a clean gradient: option 1 strengthens Prop 13 protections for commercial property, option 3 is a targeted reform applying only to very large holdings (the small-business carve-out model from Prop 15), and option 5 is a full market-value split-roll. Residential Prop 13 protections are not at issue here — every option leaves them intact.

issues.name: Utility rate regulation
issues.short_description: How much should the state step in to control electricity, gas, and insurance rates?
issues.ca_specific_context: PG&E, SCE, SDG&E rates have risen sharply; CPUC reform and proposals to replace investor-owned utilities are active debate.

Create a public option or break up the big utilities

voter_guide.current_policy: California's three big investor-owned utilities — PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E — charge some of the highest electricity rates in the country. The federal Energy Information Administration puts the statewide average around 27 cents per kWh, second only to Hawaii. PG&E residential rates rose about 50% from 2020 to 2024, driven heavily by the cost of wildfire prevention and grid upgrades that the CPUC approved. In May 2024, carrying out [AB 205](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB205) (2022), the CPUC added an income-based fixed charge — a flat monthly fee tied to household income, about $24.15/month for most customers ($6 and $12 for low-income CARE/FERA enrollees). In exchange, the per-kWh rate is projected to drop 5–7 cents. It starts showing up on PG&E bills in early 2026.
key_facts: California's average electricity price is about 27 cents per kWh (per the federal EIA) — 2nd-highest among states, behind Hawaii.
PG&E residential rates rose about 50% from 2020 to 2024; households on the low-income CARE discount saw even steeper increases.
The CPUC's May 2024 income-based fixed charge is about $24.15/month (reduced to $6 or $12 for low-income tiers), in exchange for a 5–7 cents per kWh cut to usage-based rates; it rolls out in 2025–26.
Spending on wildfire prevention and grid hardening is a leading reason recent rate increases were approved.
Public utilities like SMUD (Sacramento) and LADWP (Los Angeles) usually charge well below IOU rates, fueling debate over public-power alternatives.
voter_guide.comparison: California's IOU rates are far above the U.S. average (around 17 cents per kWh) and most peer states; only Hawaii is consistently higher. Its income-based fixed charge is the first in the nation to tie part of the bill to a household's income instead of how much power it uses.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who want stronger consumer protection argue that IOU rates have risen far faster than inflation while the utilities still earn guaranteed profits for shareholders. They say the CPUC too easily lets utilities pass wildfire and infrastructure costs to customers, and that high rates undercut the very switch to electric appliances and cars the state is requiring. They point to public utilities like SMUD, which deliver lower rates, as proof that structural reform — even having the public take over the utility — could cut bills.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who defend the current cost-recovery approach argue that wildfire hardening, grid upgrades, and storm resilience are real, necessary costs that someone has to pay — and skimping on them risks blackouts and catastrophic fires. They say utilities need predictable profits to attract the money for those investments, and that aggressive rate caps could hurt reliability or just shift costs onto taxpayers. They add that targeted discounts (CARE/FERA) and the new income-based fixed charge already protect low-income customers without tearing up the whole system.
voter_guide.note_on_options: This is a balancing scale, not a simple more/less axis: option 1 favors utility financial health and full cost recovery, option 5 favors aggressive consumer relief (rate cuts, equity adjustments, public power). The income-graduated fixed charge is contested across the spectrum — some see it as equity-promoting (higher end), others as a new fixed cost that weakens conservation incentives (lower end).

issues.name: Policing and criminal penalties
issues.short_description: How should California balance more police, police reform, and non-police alternatives?
issues.ca_specific_context: Fentanyl deaths, retail-theft enforcement, and police oversight debates have all driven CA policy since 2024.

stance_scale.label: Expand police and toughen criminal penalties
Expand police, with some reforms
Do both — more officers and more accountability and alternatives
Prioritize reform, oversight, and non-police responses
Shift significant funding from police to community services

voter_guide.current_policy: California has passed a series of police-accountability laws while leaving most funding and prosecution decisions to local agencies and elected district attorneys. [AB 392](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB392) (2019) raised the bar for when police can use deadly force — to when it's "necessary" to stop an immediate threat, instead of the older, looser "reasonable" standard. [SB 2](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB2) (2021), the Kenneth Ross Jr. Police Decertification Act, set up a statewide process to strip ("decertify") officers of their license for serious misconduct and report those who leave to a national database. [AB 1506](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1506) (2020) requires the state Department of Justice to investigate police shootings that kill unarmed civilians. The state prison population has dropped sharply since the 2011 "Realignment" ([AB 109](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201120120AB109)) shifted lower-level felons from state prisons to counties.
key_facts: [AB 392](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB392) (2019) set a "necessary" standard for police deadly force — one of the stricter use-of-force laws in the country.

[SB 2](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB2) (2021) gave the state's police-standards board (POST) the power to decertify officers for serious misconduct. Decertified officers can't be rehired and are listed on the National Decertification Index.

[AB 1506](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1506) (2020) requires the state Department of Justice to investigate fatal police shootings of unarmed civilians.

California's prison population fell to about 90,600 by December 2025 — roughly 27% below December 2019 — after the 2011 Realignment ([AB 109](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201120120AB109)) and pandemic-era reductions. The state has closed multiple prisons.

California's imprisonment rate was about 294 per 100,000 adults in 2025, down from a peak of over 173,000 total prisoners in 2006. Police staffing and budgets are set locally, so a governor's direct control is limited.
voter_guide.comparison: California's "necessary" use-of-force standard and statewide decertification system are stronger than those in many states, though states like Colorado and New Jersey adopted similar reforms after 2020. California's imprisonment rate sits near or a bit below the national average — and well below high-incarceration states like Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who favor reducing incarceration and using alternatives argue that California's prison population dropped a lot after Realignment without a lasting rise in violent crime — suggesting many people can be safely supervised in their communities. They say diversion programs, mental-health and addiction treatment, and reentry help address root causes more cheaply than prison, and that strong accountability rules (AB 392, SB 2) build community trust and cut down on costly misconduct.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who favor more funding and stricter penalties argue that having enough officers and clear consequences deters crime and reassures victims. They note that some types of crime rose during the reform years and say visible enforcement is needed for public confidence. They warn that accountability mandates and lower incarceration, if not matched with enough police and supervision resources, can strain departments and let repeat offenders cycle through. In their view, public safety shouldn't be traded away to lower prison numbers.
voter_guide.note_on_options: Policing budgets and most charging decisions are local, so a governor's levers are statewide standards, CDCR operations, prison capacity, grants, and bill signings. Stance 1 (more funding, stricter penalties) and stance 5 (decarceration, alternatives) describe direction and emphasis a governor can push, not unilateral control over local police forces or county jails.

issues.short_description: California voters recently toughened penalties for some theft and drug crimes (Prop 36, 2024). Should the state go further, keep those changes, or return to the more lenient earlier approach (Prop 47)?

voter_guide.current_policy: [Prop 47](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2014/prop-47-110414.aspx) (November 2014) reclassified several nonviolent drug-possession and theft crimes from felonies to misdemeanors — including setting the felony shoplifting/theft line at $950 — and put the savings toward treatment and victim programs. [Prop 36](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2024/Prop36-110524.pdf) (November 2024), which passed about 70% to 30% and took effect December 18, 2024, partly rolled that back. It allows felony charges for petty theft when someone has two or more prior theft convictions, lets prosecutors add up the value of multiple thefts to cross the $950 line, raises penalties for certain fentanyl and other drug crimes, and creates a "treatment-mandated felony" that gives repeat drug offenders a choice between treatment and incarceration.
key_facts: [Prop 47](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2014/prop-47-110414.aspx) (2014) set the felony theft line at $950 and dropped certain drug-possession and theft felonies to misdemeanors.
[Prop 36](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2024/Prop36-110524.pdf) (2024) passed about 70% to 30% and took effect December 18, 2024.
Prop 36 allows felony charges for theft under $950 when the person has two or more prior theft convictions, and lets values from multiple incidents be added together.

Per PPIC, California's 2024 property-crime rate fell about 9.9% to roughly 2,084 per 100,000 — its lowest since 1985 — while reported shoplifting rose about 14.2% (combined retail theft up about 3%). These trends came before Prop 36 took effect.

PPIC research credits the post-2019 rise in retail theft more to pandemic-era criminal-justice responses than to Prop 47 itself, and finds that a higher chance of getting caught deters crime more than longer sentences do.
voter_guide.comparison: After Prop 47, California's $950 felony-theft line was in the middle of the national range — higher than states like New Jersey ($200) but lower than the misdemeanor ceiling in Texas, which uses graduated tiers (felonies start around $2,500). Prop 36 didn't lower the dollar figure; instead it narrowed the misdemeanor rule for repeat offenders. Many states revisited their theft and drug-sentencing thresholds in the 2020s.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who want to keep or expand Prop 47 argue that property crime hit multi-decade lows in 2024 even before Prop 36 took effect, that lower incarceration freed up money for treatment and victim services, and that PPIC and other research find certainty of getting caught deters crime more than longer sentences. So, they argue, more decriminalization and diversion could lower incarceration without raising crime.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who want to roll back further argue that reported shoplifting and some retail thefts kept climbing after 2019, and that the $950 misdemeanor line let repeat offenders dodge real consequences. They say Prop 36's nearly 70% approval shows broad public worry about open drug use and theft, and that felony exposure for repeat offenders — plus treatment-mandated felonies — gives leverage to push chronic offenders into treatment and to deter organized retail theft.
voter_guide.note_on_options: Both measures were enacted by voters, so most changes to Prop 36 or Prop 47 require another ballot measure or a high legislative threshold — a governor mainly shapes implementation, funding, and DA/CDCR guidance and can advocate for or against future measures. Crime-trend data is genuinely contested: property crime fell in 2024 while shoplifting rose, and analysts disagree on how much Prop 47 versus pandemic-era factors drove the changes.

issues.name: Sanctuary and immigration enforcement
issues.short_description: How much should California cooperate with federal immigration enforcement (ICE)?
issues.ca_specific_context: SB 54 (2017) limits state cooperation with ICE; under renewed federal pressure as of 2025–2026.

stance_scale.label: Cooperate fully with ICE — repeal the state's sanctuary law
Keep the sanctuary law but allow more exceptions
Keep the current sanctuary law as it is
Strengthen protections (e.g. fund legal defense for immigrants)
Go much further — add new state protections, like state IDs for all

voter_guide.current_policy: California's baseline is the California Values Act, [SB 54](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB54) (2017), in effect since January 1, 2018. It says state and local agencies can't use their staff or money to do federal civil immigration enforcement. That means they generally can't hold someone in jail just because ICE asks (called a "detainer" or hold request), can't arrest people on civil immigration warrants, and can't sign "287(g)" agreements — deals that let local officers act as immigration agents. There are exceptions: jails can tell ICE when someone is being released, or hand them over, if that person was convicted of certain serious or violent felonies listed in state law. A separate law, the TRUTH Act ([AB 2792](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201520160AB2792), 2016), says people in custody must be told about, and agree to, any ICE interview, and that local governments must hold a public meeting if they give ICE access. State prisons (CDCR) are only partly covered by SB 54 and follow their own notification rules.
key_facts: [SB 54](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB54) took effect January 1, 2018. The first Trump administration sued to block it and lost: the case was dismissed, the Ninth Circuit appeals court agreed, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear it — so the law still stands.

287(g) agreements (which deputize local officers to do immigration enforcement) are banned for California agencies under SB 54. In 2025, an attempt by Shasta County's sheriff was paused because it conflicted with state law.
SB 54's exceptions let agencies notify or hand someone to ICE if that person was convicted of specific serious or violent felonies — not for people whose only issue is their immigration status.
The TRUTH Act (2016) requires that people be told they can decline an ICE jail interview, and requires a public community meeting when local agencies give ICE access.

Sanctuary rules are mostly set by state law, so a governor's main tools are enforcement guidance, the attorney general's approach to lawsuits, prison rules, and signing or vetoing new bills — not repealing the law directly.
voter_guide.comparison: California is among the states that most limit local cooperation with immigration agents, alongside Illinois (the TRUST Act) and several others. By contrast, states like Texas (with its SB 4 law) and Florida require local agencies to cooperate with ICE and ban sanctuary policies. The federal 287(g) program had agreements with roughly 1,600 agencies nationwide by 2026 — almost none in California.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who want stronger sanctuary protections argue that keeping local police out of immigration enforcement builds trust, so immigrant crime victims and witnesses will feel safe reporting crimes. They note that ICE detainers usually aren't signed by a judge, which raises constitutional concerns and can expose counties to lawsuits. And they point out that the existing felony exceptions already allow cooperation in the most serious cases — so further steps (like limiting data sharing, or keeping ICE out of courthouses, schools, and hospitals) would only affect civil enforcement.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who want fuller cooperation with ICE argue that releasing people ICE has flagged — including some with past criminal records that don't fit the exceptions — can send people federal authorities believe are deportable back into communities. They say planned handoffs from jail are safer for officers and the public than ICE making arrests out on the street, and that immigration enforcement is a federal job the state shouldn't get in the way of. In their view, turning down ICE requests hurts public safety and federal-state teamwork.
voter_guide.note_on_options: Because SB 54 is statute and was upheld in court, the realistic range for a governor runs from enforcement/guidance that maximizes the felony carve-outs (lower end) to signing bills that narrow data sharing or ICE facility access (higher end). Wholesale repeal (well below stance 1) or fully abolishing all cooperation (above stance 5) would require legislative action a governor cannot take alone.

issues.short_description: What role should natural gas play as California shifts to cleaner energy?

voter_guide.current_policy: California still gets about 40% of its in-state electricity from natural gas, and gas heats most of its roughly 14 million homes. But the state is steering new buildings toward electric power instead. In 2022, the California Air Resources Board (CARB — the state's air-quality agency) set a goal: by 2030, every new furnace and water heater sold for homes should be zero-emission, with commercial buildings following by 2035. CARB is still writing the actual rule to make that happen. It scaled the rule back in December 2025, and a board vote is expected in 2026, but nothing is final yet. Meanwhile, dozens of cities banned gas in new construction after Berkeley did so in 2019 — until a 2023 federal appeals court ruling (CRA v. Berkeley) said federal appliance law overrides those local bans. So the state has shifted to using building codes and emissions standards instead.
key_facts: About 40% of California's electricity comes from natural gas, and gas heats most of the state's homes and water.
CARB's 2022 plan aims for 100% of new home furnaces and water heaters sold to be zero-emission by 2030 — but the rule to enforce it isn't finished, and was scaled back in December 2025.
A 2023 federal appeals court ruling (CRA v. Berkeley) said local bans on gas hookups in new buildings are overridden by federal appliance law.
California offers rebates for heat pumps (electric heating-and-cooling units) through TECH Clean California and utility programs, aiming for 6 million installed by 2030.

Aliso Canyon — the gas storage site of the 2015–16 SoCalGas methane blowout, the largest in U.S. history — is still running. A once-planned 2027 closure is now not expected until the late 2030s at the earliest.
voter_guide.comparison: California is one of the most aggressive states on switching buildings off gas, alongside New York (which banned gas in most new buildings starting 2026) and Washington. Most states have gone the other way: more than 20 have passed laws that bar cities from restricting natural gas hookups.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: Supporters of moving off gas faster say buildings are a big source of greenhouse gases and smog-forming pollution, and that burning gas indoors raises health concerns. They argue that building new gas pipes and hookups is risky because that equipment could become worthless as the grid goes electric. They point out that heat pumps now beat gas furnaces in most California climates. And they warn that as fewer customers use gas, the fixed cost of maintaining the pipe network falls on the people left behind — often lower-income households — so a planned, orderly switch is cheaper than a chaotic one.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: Supporters of keeping gas as a bridge say gas can be switched on instantly to back up solar and wind when those aren't available, helping prevent blackouts at peak demand. They argue that forcing everyone to go electric raises upfront costs for families and strains a grid that's already expensive. With California electricity rates the 2nd-highest in the nation, they say the money saved by running a heat pump is uncertain. And they warn that sudden mandates outrun the electrical-panel upgrades and trained workforce needed to install millions of heat pumps.
voter_guide.note_on_options: This scale measures the pace of moving off gas, not whether to decarbonize at all — nearly all candidates accept the state's long-run carbon-neutrality goal. The disagreement is over timeline and mandates (appliance bans, hookup bans, gas-system retirement) versus incentives and voluntary adoption.

issues.name: Oil and gas production in CA
issues.short_description: Should California drill for more oil and gas in-state, keep current levels, or wind it down?
issues.ca_specific_context: SB 1137 (2022) established 3,200-ft setbacks; ballot fight overturned and re-affirmed; Kern County is the production heartland.

Keep current production; ease regulations
Keep things roughly as they are
Wind it down — tighten rules, stop issuing new drilling permits

voter_guide.current_policy: California allows oil and gas drilling within the state, but it has tightened the rules and isn't approving much new drilling. [SB 1137](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB1137) (Gonzalez, 2022) bans new or reworked wells within 3,200 feet of homes, schools, hospitals, and other places where people spend a lot of time. The oil industry tried to overturn the law with a ballot referendum, but withdrew it on June 26, 2024 — so the buffer-zone law took effect instead of going to voters as a 2024 ballot measure. In-state oil production has dropped sharply: California pumped about 104 million barrels of crude in 2024, down roughly 70% from its peak. And CARB's Low Carbon Fuel Standard — a state rule that pushes transportation fuels to produce less carbon, amended in 2024 and effective July 2025 — keeps tightening those targets.
key_facts: [SB 1137](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB1137)'s 3,200-foot buffer between new wells and homes took effect June 27, 2024 after the industry withdrew its repeal referendum. It was NOT passed as a 'Prop 4' ballot measure — that's a common mix-up.
California produced about 104 million barrels of crude in 2024 — down roughly 70% from its peak. The state ranks about 7th among U.S. oil producers.
Kern County accounts for roughly 65–70% of California's in-state oil production.
California imports most of the crude its refineries use — only about a quarter comes from in-state wells. The rest arrives by sea or from Alaska.

CARB's 2024 update to the Low Carbon Fuel Standard (a rule that requires transportation fuels to get cleaner over time; effective July 1, 2025) tightened the targets. CARB estimated it would add about 5–8 cents per gallon in the near term, though some academic estimates were higher.
voter_guide.comparison: California is the only major U.S. oil-producing state that pairs large output with a stated plan to wind production down. Texas, New Mexico, and North Dakota are all expanding. California's 3,200-foot buffer between new wells and homes is among the largest required drilling setbacks in the country.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: Supporters of phasing out oil faster say drilling concentrates air pollution and health harms in low-income and Latino communities near the wells. They note that in-state production is already shrinking and supplies only a minority of the crude California refines — so winding it down in an orderly way would have limited effect on supply. They argue that continued drilling clashes with the state's carbon-neutrality goal, and that every new well adds to the pile of abandoned, idle wells the state will eventually have to pay to clean up.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: Supporters of keeping production say in-state oil supports tens of thousands of jobs and a big share of Kern County's tax base. They argue that cutting local supply means importing more crude — often produced under weaker environmental rules elsewhere — and leaves drivers exposed to price spikes. They warn that refinery closures already threaten fuel supply and prices, and that sudden restrictions push up gas prices in a state that already has among the nation's highest prices at the pump.
voter_guide.note_on_options: The scale runs from expanding production (1) to rapid statewide phaseout (5). 'Status quo' sits near the middle: California currently allows existing production to continue and decline while restricting new wells near communities. A candidate who supports SB 1137 setbacks but opposes a hard end-date for extraction codes around 3.

issues.name: K-12 school funding and governance
issues.short_description: Should California spend more, less, or about the same on K-12 public schools?
issues.ca_specific_context: Prop 98 (1988) sets a minimum funding floor; LCFF (2013) restructured allocation around student need.

stance_scale.label: Cut K-12 spending significantly
Trim or hold spending
Keep spending about the same
Increase funding modestly (teacher pay, facilities)
Increase funding a lot (teacher pay, smaller classes), raising new revenue if needed

voter_guide.current_policy: K-12 funding rests on two pillars. [Prop 98](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) (1988) is a constitutional rule that sets a yearly minimum the state must spend on schools and community colleges. The Local Control Funding Formula (LCFF, 2013) decides how that money is split: every district gets a base grant per student, plus a supplemental grant (an extra 20% of the base) and, for districts with lots of high-need students, a concentration grant — all aimed at students who are low-income, learning English, or in foster care. For 2024-25, the Prop 98 minimum was about $115.3 billion total (roughly $101.1 billion for K-12). Voters also passed [Prop 2](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2024) in November 2024, a $10 billion bond to build and fix school and community-college buildings.
key_facts: Total spending per student from all sources was about $23,878 for 2024-25 (state estimate), and is projected to keep rising.
On apples-to-apples Census figures, California spent about $19,894 per student in 2022-23 — roughly 13th among the states, up from 28th the year before.
LCFF (2013) stacks a supplemental grant (an extra 20% of the base) and a concentration grant on top of each district's base grant to steer more money to higher-need districts.

On the 2024 NAEP national test, California scored just below the national average — for example, 4th-grade reading 212 vs. 214 and 8th-grade reading 254 vs. 257 — though its long-run gap with the rest of the country has narrowed.

[Prop 2](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2024) (November 2024) authorized $10 billion in bonds for K-12 and community-college buildings; many districts also charge local parcel taxes (a flat tax on each property), which need two-thirds voter approval.
voter_guide.comparison: Once you adjust for California's high costs, its per-student spending now sits in the upper-middle of the states, though still below big spenders like New York. Its NAEP scores still come in below the national average, which keeps the debate alive over whether the problem is too few dollars, how the dollars get spent, or a lack of accountability.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who want more funding and stronger local control say California still spends less per student than comparable high-cost states, and that LCFF's supplemental and concentration grants should be bigger to close opportunity gaps for low-income students, English learners, and foster youth. They argue a steady, dedicated source of money — a tax or a bond — is needed for competitive teacher pay, school buildings, and expanding transitional kindergarten, and that local educators, not Sacramento mandates, know best how to spend it.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who stress accountability and reform say spending has climbed a lot since LCFF without matching gains on NAEP, so the priority should be showing where the concentration-grant money actually goes and getting measurable results — not new taxes. They note that [Prop 98](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) already guarantees a rising floor, that the state budget swings with the economy, and that LCFF's loose spending rules make it hard to confirm the extra money is reaching the high-need students it's meant for.
voter_guide.note_on_options: The scale spans both the funding level (cut to major new revenue) and the state-vs-local control axis. These can diverge: a candidate might favor more local control without a tax increase, or more state-directed equity funding. Our default coding treats support for a dedicated new tax or bond as the strongest value-5 signal and an accountability-first, reform-LCFF posture as value 1.

voter_guide.explainer: A few terms come up a lot here. 'Prop 98' is a 1988 amendment to the state constitution that sets a yearly minimum the state must spend on K-12 schools and community colleges. 'LCFF,' the Local Control Funding Formula, is the 2013 system for handing out that money: every district gets a base amount per student, plus extra for students who are low-income, learning English, or in foster care. A 'parcel tax' is a flat local tax on each property that some districts use to raise extra school money.

issues.name: School choice and charters
issues.short_description: Should California make it easier or harder to open charter schools and give families more school choices?
issues.ca_specific_context: AB 1505 (2019) gave districts more charter denial authority; vouchers have repeatedly failed at the ballot.

stance_scale.label: Open many more charter schools and expand family choice
Open more charter schools; protect family choice
Keep the current charter school rules about the same
Make it harder to open new charter schools
Stop new charter schools; send the money to traditional public schools

voter_guide.current_policy: California has about 1,283 charter schools, plus seven districts made up entirely of charters (state data, May 2024). They teach roughly 11.7% of public-school students. Two 2019 laws — [AB 1505](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1505) and [AB 1507](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1507), both signed that October and effective July 1, 2020 — made it harder to open and renew charters. Districts can now turn down a new charter by pointing to the financial hit or community impact, charters generally can't run campuses outside the district that approved them, and a low-performing charter can be denied renewal. California offers no state-funded private-school vouchers or education savings accounts. (A voucher gives families public money to spend on private-school tuition; an education savings account, or ESA, is a government-funded account parents can spend on tuition, tutoring, or other approved education costs.) The last voucher measure, [Prop 38](https://www.lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/38_11_2000.html) in 2000, lost 71% to 29%.
key_facts: About 1,283 charter schools and 7 all-charter districts were operating in California (state data, May 2024); charters teach roughly 11.7% of public-school students (2022-23).

[AB 1505](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1505) (2019) ended the old near-automatic right to appeal a rejected charter, and let districts cite the financial hit and community need when turning down or refusing to renew one.

[AB 1507](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1507) (2019) stopped most new charters from running learning centers or satellite campuses outside the district that approved them (the 'charter authorizer' — the agency, usually a school district, that grants and oversees the charter).
Charter enrollment has ticked up while regular district enrollment has fallen, partly because total statewide enrollment is dropping.

[Prop 38](https://www.lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/38_11_2000.html) (2000), which would have given families a voucher of about $4,000 per child, lost 71% to 29%. No statewide voucher has reached the ballot since.
voter_guide.comparison: California is one of the stricter big states on school choice: it has a large charter sector but, unlike Arizona, Florida, or Indiana, offers no private-school vouchers or education savings accounts. Its 2019 laws cut against the national trend, which has been toward expanding private-school choice.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who want more choice say charters give families — disproportionately lower-income families and families of color — an option besides their assigned neighborhood school, and that some charter networks get strong results for those students. They argue [AB 1505](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1505) gave districts a money-based reason to block competitors, and that vouchers or education savings accounts would open up choice to families who can't afford private tuition or a move into a top-rated school zone.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: Opponents — including the California Teachers Association (CTA) and the California School Boards Association (CSBA) — say charters and vouchers pull per-pupil dollars (the funding that follows each student) away from district schools, which still teach most kids and still have fixed bills to pay. They argue charter quality is uneven and oversight is weaker, point to research (such as Stanford's CREDO studies) showing charter results vary a lot by operator and state, and note that California voters have repeatedly rejected vouchers as using public money to pay for private and religious schools.
voter_guide.note_on_options: The scale blends two distinct mechanisms: charter policy (a public-school option) and private-school vouchers/ESAs (public funds for private tuition). A candidate can favor charter expansion while opposing vouchers, or vice versa. Our default coding treats support for vouchers as the strongest pro-choice signal (value 1) and a cap-and-redirect posture as the strongest restrictive signal (value 5).

issues.name: Healthcare funding mechanism
issues.short_description: Should California move toward a state-run, single-payer health system (the state covers everyone instead of private insurance) — and if so, how would it be paid for?
issues.ca_specific_context: AB 1400 / CalCare proposals have repeatedly stalled over funding; Medi-Cal was expanded to undocumented adults in 2024.

stance_scale.label: Roll back recent expansions of state health coverage (Medi-Cal)
Keep today's system; focus on lowering costs
Expand coverage gradually, without a big new tax
Single-payer, paid for mainly by taxes on wealth and corporations
Single-payer, paid for by broad new taxes (such as a payroll tax)

voter_guide.current_policy: California uses a mix of private insurance plus heavy government help, rather than one state-run plan. Covered California is the state's Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace, where people buy coverage, and the state chips in to lower premiums. Medi-Cal — California's version of Medicaid, the public coverage program for low-income residents — was expanded on January 1, 2024 to cover all eligible undocumented adults, making California the first state to offer full Medicaid coverage no matter someone's immigration status. Efforts to switch to a single government-run plan have repeatedly failed: [AB 1400](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB1400) (the CalCare bill, 2022) was withdrawn before a vote, and its follow-up, [AB 2200](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB2200) (2024), was stopped in committee.
key_facts: Medi-Cal extended full coverage to all eligible adults regardless of immigration status on January 1, 2024 — the first state to do so.

[AB 1400](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB1400) (CalCare) died on January 31, 2022 when its author pulled it, short of the 41 Assembly votes it needed. Its 2024 follow-up, [AB 2200](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB2200), was held up in the Appropriations committee.
Analysts estimated CalCare would cost roughly $314–391 billion a year — more than the state's entire general-fund budget — and would require new payroll, business, and high-income taxes.

A single-payer plan would need the federal government to sign off (through what are called Section 1332 and Medicaid/Medicare waivers) to redirect federal money. A federal law called ERISA also limits how much a state can regulate the self-funded health plans that many large employers use.
California's uninsured rate dropped to about 6–7% in recent years — among the lowest ever — thanks to ACA subsidies and the Medi-Cal expansion, not a single-payer system.
voter_guide.comparison: No U.S. state runs a single-payer system. Vermont passed one in 2014, then dropped it because it couldn't figure out how to pay for it. California chose a different path — expanding subsidies and Medicaid — and got to one of the lowest uninsured rates in the country while keeping the private insurance market in place.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who want to move toward a state single-payer plan (the high end) say one public plan would cut out insurance-company overhead, premiums, deductibles, and limited provider networks. They point to some analyses (such as a UC Berkeley Labor Center estimate) that projected the whole system could spend less overall. They argue that covering everyone — regardless of job or immigration status — is simpler to run, and that California's sheer size would give it leverage to negotiate lower prices.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who want to keep the current subsidized private market (the low end) say single-payer's roughly $300–400 billion-a-year price tag would mean steep new taxes, with no guarantee of net savings. They note it depends on federal sign-offs and ERISA exceptions that might never come. They warn that upending the employer and Medicare coverage most people already have is risky, both politically and practically — and that California already reached near-universal coverage by expanding subsidies and Medi-Cal without that upheaval.
voter_guide.note_on_options: This scale measures the financing mechanism — from preserving a subsidized private market (1) to a state-run single-payer plan like CalCare (5) — not whether to expand coverage. A candidate can favor broad coverage expansion (e.g., the 2024 Medi-Cal expansion) while opposing single-payer financing; such positions land in the middle of the scale.

issues.name: Abortion and reproductive rights
issues.short_description: Should California expand, keep, or restrict abortion access?
issues.ca_specific_context: Prop 1 (2022) enshrined abortion rights in the CA Constitution; CA has funded travel for out-of-state patients.

stance_scale.label: Add restrictions (such as time limits or parental consent)
Allow some restrictions
Keep California's current strong protections
Strengthen access — more funding and more providers
Go further — fund out-of-state patients and broaden who can provide care

voter_guide.current_policy: Abortion is a right written into California's constitution. [Proposition 1](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2022) (November 2022), approved by about 66% of voters, amended the state constitution to bar California from denying or interfering with reproductive freedom, including abortion and contraception. After the U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 Dobbs decision ended the federal right to abortion, the Legislature passed a set of laws. [AB 1242](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB1242) and [AB 2091](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2091) (2022) stop California police, businesses, and providers from helping with out-of-state abortion investigations or handing over related records. [SB 345](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB345) (2023) protects California-licensed providers — including those offering telehealth and abortion pills — from being prosecuted or extradited by other states. Medi-Cal covers abortion at full state cost, and the state has set aside more than $200 million to support abortion access and providers.
key_facts: [Proposition 1](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2022) (2022) passed with about 66% support, writing an explicit right to abortion and contraception into the state constitution.
Medi-Cal covers abortion with the state paying the full cost, and private insurance plans regulated by the state are generally required to cover it too.

California passed shield laws — [AB 1242](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB1242), [AB 2091](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2091) (2022) and [SB 345](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB345) (2023) — that protect in-state providers and patients (including out-of-state patients using telehealth) from being pulled into other states' abortion prosecutions.
The state has set aside more than $200 million across recent budgets to fund abortion access, expand provider capacity, and help patients with costs such as travel.
After Dobbs, California set itself up as a place patients from states with bans could travel to for care, with state funding to support them.
voter_guide.comparison: California is one of the most protective states for abortion access after Dobbs, pairing a constitutional right, Medi-Cal coverage, public funding, and provider shield laws. That stands in sharp contrast to the more than a dozen states that ban or sharply restrict abortion, and puts California in a small group of states that openly fund and protect care for patients coming from elsewhere.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who want to expand protections further (the high end) say that as more states impose bans, California should act as a refuge — funding travel and care for out-of-state patients, broadening provider protections and capacity, and getting ahead of any future federal limits. They argue that cost and logistics, not just whether something is legal, decide whether people can actually get care, so the state should fund and shield it aggressively.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who favor some limits, or simply not expanding further (the low end), argue on moral or religious grounds that abortion should face some restrictions, such as limits later in pregnancy. They say public money shouldn't pay for abortion or for out-of-state patients' care, and that shield laws and refuge funding drag California into fights with other states' laws and stretch what taxpayers are asked to cover. Within California, this is a minority view given Prop 1's 66% margin.
voter_guide.note_on_options: This scale runs from supporting some restrictions on access (1) to an expansive state-funded interstate refuge with broad provider protections (5). Given California's constitutional right and lopsided 2022 vote, most viable candidates cluster toward the protective end; the differentiating questions are about how far to fund interstate care and shield providers, not whether abortion is legal in-state.

issues.name: Gun policy
issues.short_description: Should California's gun laws be loosened, kept the same, or made stricter?
issues.ca_specific_context: CA's assault-weapons ban, magazine limits, and CCW frameworks have been in continuous litigation since Bruen (2022).

stance_scale.label: Loosen them significantly (easier concealed carry, lighter enforcement)
Loosen some specific rules
Keep current gun laws as they are
Defend current laws and close loopholes
Add major new restrictions (gun registry, more bans)

voter_guide.current_policy: California has some of the strictest gun laws in the country. The Roberti-Roos Assault Weapons Control Act (1989) and later laws ban many semiautomatic "assault weapons," and the state caps magazines at 10 rounds. In 2022, the U.S. Supreme Court case NYSRPA v. Bruen struck down rules that let officials decide who had a "good enough reason" to carry a concealed gun. In response, [SB 2](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB2) (2023, effective January 1, 2024) switched California to "shall-issue" permits — meaning anyone who qualifies gets one — while adding a 16-hour training requirement and a long list of "sensitive places" where guns are banned even with a permit. A separate law, [AB 28](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB28) (2023, effective 2024), added an 11% state tax on gun and ammunition sales to fund violence-prevention and school-safety programs.
key_facts: California has banned "assault weapons" since the 1989 Roberti-Roos Act and limits magazines to 10 rounds.

[SB 2](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB2) (effective January 1, 2024) kept shall-issue permits after the Bruen ruling but named about 26 categories of "sensitive places." In 2025 the Ninth Circuit appeals court upheld some of those location bans and blocked others while the case continues.

[AB 28](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB28)'s 11% tax on guns and ammunition (effective 2024) is projected to raise about $160 million a year for violence-prevention and school-safety programs. It faces an unresolved court challenge.

Microstamping and other manufacturer-side rules (such as [SB 452](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB452), 2023) are still on the books, though some parts only kick in if the technology is found workable.

Several California gun laws are in active litigation in the Ninth Circuit under the Bruen test — which asks whether a law fits the nation's "history and tradition" of gun regulation — so which rules can actually be enforced shifts as courts rule.
voter_guide.comparison: Independent and advocacy scorecards consistently rank California's gun laws the strictest, or nearly the strictest, in the country — alongside Massachusetts, New York, Illinois, and Connecticut. By contrast, "constitutional carry" states like Texas, Arizona, and Idaho require no permit to carry a concealed gun and have far fewer limits on magazines and rifle types.
voter_guide.arguments_for_change: People who want more restrictions point out that states with stronger gun laws tend to report lower gun-death rates. They argue that the assault-weapon and magazine limits, SB 2's sensitive-places list, and the AB 28 tax cut down gun availability in risky settings while paying for prevention. They say closing remaining gaps — and defending current laws in court — saves lives, and that the Second Amendment still allows reasonable regulation.
voter_guide.arguments_against_change: People who oppose more restrictions argue that California already has the nation's strictest rules yet still has gun crime, so the payoff from new limits is small. They say the post-Bruen court rulings suggest several of California's laws may be unconstitutional and invite expensive lawsuits. They argue that broad sensitive-place bans and a sales tax burden law-abiding gun owners and make carry rights depend on where you are. And they say enforcement is better aimed at illegal trafficking and people already barred from owning guns than at lawful buyers.
voter_guide.note_on_options: Much of California's gun law is shaped by Ninth Circuit and Supreme Court litigation, so a governor's practical range runs from defending or narrowing existing rules in light of court rulings (lower end) to signing new restrictions and aggressively defending them (higher end). 'Rolling back' (stance 1) would primarily mean declining to defend or signing repeals, both constrained by the Legislature.

positions.source_quote: Republican Steve Hilton warned that SB 79 will 'destroy' California's 'single-family suburban neighborhoods' by allowing the construction of mid-rise apartment buildings. The former Fox News host objects to state-led planning mandates and to the prevailing orthodoxy among YIMBY-aligned Democrats in Sacramento that the state should focus new construction in dense urban areas.
positions.notes: Stance 4 (slow growth / protect neighborhood character) is the best fit because while Hilton talks about building more, he opposes the main tool the state has to actually preempt the local 'no' (SB 79) and frames the issue as defending suburbs. His own site uses 'war on single family homes' and 'Restore the California Dream of a single family home for every family.'

positions.summary: Steyer pledged to build one million homes in four years and was one of two leading Democrats (with Porter) who publicly championed SB 79 during the legislative fight, not just after signing. He explicitly endorses state intervention when localities block housing.
positions.source_quote: The state has passed critical laws to streamline permitting, increase density, and prioritize housing near transit, which I championed (SB 79) and helped lobby to pass... if local governments refuse to follow the law and seek to block housing, the state will step in.
positions.notes: California YIMBY characterizes Steyer as 'a vocal, public supporter of SB 79 throughout the legislative fight,' showing up when it was politically costly. The 'one million homes over four years' number comes directly from his housing plan page.

positions.summary: Bianco's housing platform is pure deregulation: eliminate CEQA, expedite permits, incentivize builders, and defend Prop 13. He has not endorsed state preemption of local zoning, and California YIMBY says he has 'said little on housing other than blaming his political opponents.'
positions.source_quote: Expedite approval for housing projects... Eliminate CEQA and the litigation that only passes costs onto the homebuyer... End the over regulation of our building industry... Incentivize developers to build across California.
positions.notes: Stance 3 ('build with balance, local control preserved') is the best available fit: he wants more supply via deregulation but is silent on state zoning preemption and defends Prop 13/local primacy. His housing page is thin and CalMatters did not document a position from him on SB 79.

positions.summary: Becerra would treat housing as essential infrastructure, declare a housing state of emergency on day one, and expand SB 79 and SB 684 to end exclusionary zoning beyond transit areas. He explicitly says communities should have a voice but 'not a veto.'
positions.source_quote: Last year's SB 79 created the zoning for more housing, especially affordable housing, near rail transit... Communities should have a voice in this process but they should not have a veto over the obligation.
positions.notes: Becerra's platform language is explicitly preemption-friendly ('not a veto'), pushing stance toward 1. California YIMBY notes he came to housing late as a campaign priority and only endorsed SB 79 after Newsom signed it, so he's slightly less proven on the fight than Steyer/Porter, but his published platform is firmly in the aggressive-preemption camp.

positions.summary: Porter publicly backed SB 79 during the legislative fight (including breaking with skilled-labor language) and centers her housing plan on shaving two years off construction timelines and bringing apartment costs down 20%, including by stopping local delays after entitlement.
positions.source_quote: I disagree on SB79. I support it and was glad to see @CA_Dem endorse it this weekend. Workers, students, seniors and other Californians will all benefit from more housing—especially near transit.
positions.notes: Porter is grouped with Steyer as one of the two Dems who publicly supported SB 79 'when it mattered.' Her own site emphasizes supply acceleration ('speed up building by nearly two years', 'stopping local delays that too often occur even after the projects receive a building entitlement'). The tweet date is approximated to August 2025 around when CA Dems endorsed SB 79; URL is verbatim from the search result.

positions.summary: Mahan has the strongest production track record of any candidate — his San Jose fee reform turned zero market-rate starts into ~2,000 ground-breakings — and supports deregulation, capped local fees, and code reform. But he conspicuously did not endorse SB 79 and previously opposed SB 9, making him noticeably more cautious on outright state zoning preemption than Steyer/Porter/Becerra.
positions.source_quote: As Mayor, Matt Mahan cut excessive regulation and red tape – as a result, San Jose has built new homes for the first time in years and lowered housing costs.
positions.notes: Despite the YIMBY-friendly press, California YIMBY explicitly observes: 'Mayor Mahan didn't endorse SB 79, and stopped shy of calling out zoning as the problem almost every time.' He opposed SB 9. That puts him at 2 (strong state targets and supply push, but modest rather than aggressive preemption of local zoning), not 1.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa pairs CEQA modernization, streamlined permits, and a Housing Production Accountability Board to enforce RHNA targets with a $25B revenue-bond Middle-Class Homeownership Act aimed at financing 100,000–150,000 new middle-income homes. Heavy on supply and accountability, but with less explicit endorsement of zoning preemption than Becerra/Steyer/Porter.
positions.source_quote: Reforming CEQA, streamlining permits, and enforcing production accountability can close the gap between planning and building... As a temporary situation, I'm for [rent control]... if you want to bring down rents over the long term, you need supply.
positions.notes: Stance 2 (strong state targets, modest preemption) fits: his plan emphasizes RHNA enforcement and supply, but the policy levers are CEQA/permit reform and homebuyer financing rather than an explicit SB 79-style upzoning posture. The second clause of the quote is from his CalMatters interview confirming a supply-first long-run framing.

positions.summary: Thurmond's housing pitch is built around a $10B affordable-housing bond, building up to 2 million subsidized units on surplus school-district land, down-payment assistance, and taxing corporate housing speculators. He has not articulated a position on SB 79 or local-zoning preemption.
positions.source_quote: California has 2.3 million housing units hiding in plain sight on surplus school district land sitting vacant across the state. I'm working with our top housing leaders to give school districts the startup funding they need to develop that land building homes for teachers...
positions.notes: Stance 5 (focus on subsidies and tenant-side policy rather than market supply) is the closest fit: every concrete plank is a subsidy, public-land, bond, or anti-speculator measure rather than a deregulatory or preemption lever. He hasn't taken a public SB 79 position. Stance could arguably be 3 because the school-land plan is supply-additive, but the bias is clearly subsidy-led, not preemption-led.

positions.summary: Hilton's primary lever is law enforcement: clear encampments first under Grants Pass authority, then triage. He calls Housing First a 'complete disaster' and would redirect funding to 'sober housing' with sobriety conditions, framing the status quo as a $24 billion 'catastrophic failure.'
positions.source_quote: This is against the law, and the law needs to be enforced. [Hilton] called the existing 'housing first' philosophy a 'complete disaster' and instead wants to free up all state funding to support sober housing.
positions.notes: Stance 1 (aggressive clearance) fits because removal-first is his explicit sequencing. He ducked specifics on conservatorship standards when pressed by CalMatters, so he's not as fully committed to expanded involuntary commitment as Bianco — but his enforcement-first framing and rejection of Housing First put him at the most aggressive end of the scale.

positions.summary: Steyer is 'fully committed to a Housing First approach' but pairs it with 'bridge housing with robust stabilization services' and a spending review — he treats homelessness as primarily a housing-supply and care-matching problem, not an enforcement problem. He has not endorsed sweeps or expanded conservatorship.
positions.source_quote: No one gets better on the street... [Steyer is] fully committed to a Housing First approach... matching the right housing with the right level of care.
positions.notes: Stance 4 rather than 5 because his framing leans heavily on bridge/interim housing as the urgent immediate step (a moderate position) and he wants a 'full spending review' — not a stance 5 'pour more money in' posture. He has not addressed encampment sweeps or conservatorship directly in his public platform, which lowers confidence.

positions.summary: Bianco wants the state to use Grants Pass to clear encampments, force people into treatment via new legislation, and cut off all nonprofit/HHAP funding. He rejects the 'homeless' framing entirely and claims ~95% of people on the street are addicted — the most enforcement-and-treatment-coercive platform in the field.
positions.source_quote: This is not about homes. Stop calling it homeless... We have to get to a point where the Legislature passes a law that we can actually force people into mental health treatment... No NGO and no nonprofit is going to get money with me as the governor.
positions.notes: Stance 1 is the unambiguous fit: he explicitly wants forced treatment legislation beyond what SB 43 and Prop 1 already allow, and would zero out nonprofit homelessness funding. His own platform page lists Grants Pass-based encampment clearance as Pillar 1.

positions.summary: Becerra explicitly endorses Housing First 'always paired, where needed, with behavioral health and addiction treatment,' commits to implementing every Prop 1 reform, and frames shelter as 'a bridge, not an endpoint.'
