His main innovation is accountability dashboards and tying HHAP funding to outcomes, not enforcement.
positions.source_quote: Housing First approaches, always paired, where needed, with behavioral health and addiction treatment... This is not a housing crisis alone. It is a mental health crisis... expand shelter capacity as a bridge, not an endpoint.
positions.notes: Stance 4 rather than 5 because his Prop 1 / conservatorship enthusiasm and his 'communities that fail will face real consequences' framing carry meaningful coercive edges — he isn't a pure services-only candidate. He declined to participate in the Press Democrat round-up, and his campaign page is the cleanest articulation.

positions.summary: Porter frames homelessness as 'a direct correlate of our housing problems' and emphasizes prevention (emergency rental assistance, rapid re-housing) plus interim housing as 'absolutely necessary.' She has not endorsed sweeps or expanded conservatorship and treats unsheltered status itself as a mental-health/substance-use risk factor.
positions.source_quote: It is so much more cost-effective and so much more humane to prevent families from becoming homeless in the first place... [her plan focuses on] homeless prevention through emergency rental assistance and rapid re-housing, and interim housing that can keep people from being unsheltered, which is itself a risk factor for mental health and substance use problems.
positions.notes: Stance 4 fits her prevention-and-housing-supply emphasis. Confidence is medium because she has not publicly addressed CARE Court, SB 43, or sweeps in detail — a notable gap given how prominent those debates are. If she were to articulate them, she could easily move to stance 5.

positions.summary: Mahan describes an 'all-of-the-above' approach and 'mass treatment' on his gubernatorial campaign — but his actual San Jose record is the most enforcement-forward of any Democrat in the field: his June 2025 'Responsibility to Shelter' ordinance lets the city cite and ultimately arrest unhoused people who refuse three shelter offers in 18 months. He also openly endorses 30-60 day involuntary commitment as 'a temporary suspension of certain civil liberties.'
positions.source_quote: I don't think it's humane or compassionate to allow people to live or die on our streets when they are unable or unwilling to accept the help the city is able to offer... The compassionate thing to do is to intervene. And yes, that may look like a temporary suspension of certain civil liberties.
positions.notes: GOVERNANCE-RHETORIC GAP. Mahan's gubernatorial site ('balancing compassion with accountability,' 'mass treatment not mass incarceration') reads like a stance 3. But his actual San Jose ordinance — citation on first two refusals, arrest on the third within 18 months, with explicit intent to use arrests to compel court-ordered treatment — is materially more coercive than any other Democrat in this field. Coding to the record (stance 2: enforcement-first with concurrent service offers), not the rhetoric. Santa Clara County's DA and Sheriff publicly opposed the ordinance.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa rejects criminalization ('I'm not for criminalizing homelessness. I am for compassion. But I'm not for chaos') and prioritizes housing construction (including tiny homes), but he also wants to convene experts to lower the bar for locked psychiatric conservatorship and would withhold HHAP funding from counties that underperform on CARE Court.
positions.source_quote: I'm not for criminalizing homeless(ness). I am for compassion. But I'm not for chaos... sometimes the compassionate course of action is to commit them to a locked psychiatric institution.
positions.notes: Stance 3 is the best fit because he pairs a clear anti-criminalization line with a willingness to expand involuntary commitment for severe mental illness and to use HHAP funding as a stick. The 'compassion vs chaos' framing is his deliberate middle position. His current campaign site does not foreground homelessness positions — most detail comes from the CalMatters interview.

positions.summary: Thurmond's platform is build-and-treat: 2 million affordable units on surplus school land by 2030, a $10B housing bond including tiny homes, taxing the wealthy to fund mental-health services, and conditioning housing-program participation on treatment 'if applicable.' He has not endorsed sweeps or expanded conservatorship.
positions.source_quote: [Thurmond] favors taxing the state's wealthiest residents more to pay for health care, including mental health services for those experiencing or at risk of homelessness, and he supports housing programs that require participants to undergo treatment if applicable to their situation.
positions.notes: Stance 4 fits his housing-supply-plus-services emphasis. Confidence is medium because his campaign site lacks a dedicated homelessness page — positions are reconstructed from CapRadio and Press Democrat reporting. The 'treatment if applicable' condition keeps him from a pure stance 5; he has not endorsed any specific encampment-enforcement or conservatorship-expansion position.

positions.summary: Hilton would suspend the LCFS, reformulation requirements, and 'other extreme and unnecessary refinery regulation' by executive action on Day 1, fire CARB chair Liane Randolph, and roll back cap-and-trade pass-through to drive pump prices to $3/gal. He frames LCFS as adding ~40 cents/gal with minimal environmental benefit.
positions.source_quote: Suspend the Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS), reformulation requirements, and other extreme and unnecessary refinery regulation... On Day 1 as governor I will remove Liane Randolph and start rolling back extreme climate regulations so we can have $3.00 gas.
positions.notes: The clearest stance 1 in the field — names LCFS, refinery reformulation, and cap-and-trade pass-through explicitly, with a Day 1 executive-action commitment.

positions.summary: Steyer defends California's climate framework and would attack pump prices via refinery-margin caps and accelerating alternatives — not by loosening LCFS or CARB rules. He has spent decades funding climate policy (NextGen, IRA advisory council) and frames the answer to gas prices as 'get off oil,' not as cutting LCFS. No statement found tightening LCFS specifically, so mapped to 3 rather than 4.
positions.source_quote: We need to develop alternative sources of gasoline in the state of California... The answer here is to get off oil. As I say, solar and wind don't go through the Straits of Hormuz.
positions.notes: Steyer's signature gas-price idea is the CEC 'maximum gross refining margin' penalty, which tightens oversight of refiner profits rather than fuel-carbon rules. He has not publicly proposed tightening LCFS or new refinery emissions rules in the sources reviewed; if anything, the CalMatters 2026-03 piece notes he dismissed Villaraigosa and Mahan's loosening proposals as 'unserious.' Could be argued as 4 given his EnviroVoters endorsement and climate record, but absent a verbatim 'tighten LCFS' statement, 3 is the defensible call.

positions.summary: Bianco would 'eliminate the regulations' on California's oil industry, allow expanded in-state drilling, and rescind environmental rules he says add ~$2/gal at the pump. He doesn't name LCFS as specifically as Hilton, but his framing of 'the regulations have to go away' encompasses CARB fuel rules and refinery requirements.
positions.source_quote: Gasoline, the regulations that increase it almost $2 a gallon, that will be immediately reduced... The regulations have to go away. We have to allow drilling to occur.
positions.notes: Less LCFS-specific than Hilton — his rhetoric is wholesale ('regulations have to go away') rather than itemized. Still clearly stance 1: he is the candidate who most flatly rejects the existence of California's fuel/refinery regulatory regime.

positions.summary: Becerra says he is 'open to revising the state's climate goals to keep fuel affordable for middle-class Californians' and wants to maintain refinery capacity through the transition, while still framing 'we're never going backwards.' He has not endorsed suspending LCFS but signals willingness to soften compliance costs — the most prominent centrist-Democrat 'affordability over speed' position in the field.
positions.source_quote: The most important thing we can do is stabilize... not just the price, but stabilize the supply and stabilize the distribution of gas... if you can provide some predictability, you won't see the spikes in the price of gas the way you see now.
positions.notes: Notable position to flag in the dataset. Becerra has not explicitly named LCFS in his own materials — his Energy & Utilities page focuses on utility oversight and 'affordable, reliable, fair' climate transition. The 'open to revising the state's climate goals to keep fuel affordable' phrasing is reported consistently across CalMatters and LAist voter guides, which is what places him at stance 2 rather than 3. Worth re-verifying with a direct on-record statement before publication.

positions.summary: Porter defends LCFS as part of why California has made air-quality progress and would 'stay the course' on existing refinery capacity through the transition — explicitly distinguishing keeping current refineries open from new drilling, which she opposes. She would not suspend LCFS but also has not proposed tightening it.
positions.source_quote: We are creating a lot of good, high-paying jobs in renewables, but I think we're going to have to kind of stay the course with regard to our existing refinery capacity, protecting those California jobs, keeping gas as low as we can for the foreseeable future while that transition occurs.
positions.notes: Her 'stay the course' line is sometimes misread as deregulation; in context it is about keeping existing refineries operating, not about loosening LCFS. She credited California's fuel standard for the state's air-quality progress in the same CBS interview.

positions.summary: Mahan's headline gas-price idea is a temporary suspension of the state gas tax, but he has explicitly said he 'wouldn't rule out also curbing some of the state's refinery regulations.' He frames the climate transition as needing innovation and a real cost accounting, criticizing carbon-neutrality mandates set 'without a plan to do it or the math around what it will cost people.'
positions.source_quote: Mahan supports temporarily suspending the state gas tax, but in an interview said he wouldn't rule out also curbing some of the state's refinery regulations.
positions.notes: No verbatim Mahan statement found that names LCFS specifically — the CalMatters phrasing is paraphrased but presented as his direct interview answer. Stance 2 reflects the clear 'open to curbing refinery rules' signal plus his innovation-over-mandate climate framing, while acknowledging he has been less specific than Villaraigosa.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa has called for an immediate moratorium on CARB regulations that raise consumer fuel costs by more than $0.01/gal and proposes a hard cap on LCFS credit-cost pass-through to drivers. He would 'reform and overhaul CARB' as governor and labels existing fuel-emissions rules 'failed policies.' He stops short of fully suspending LCFS — he wants a ceiling on its pass-through cost and a moratorium on new rules, not outright repeal.
positions.source_quote: Today, I am calling for an immediate moratorium on costly regulations overburdening California refineries that produce the cleanest gas in the nation and a moratorium on the costly regulations that have made the price of gas a crippling burden on working families... As Governor, I will reform and overhaul CARB...
positions.notes: Most deregulatory Democrat on this issue. Plausibly stance 1 given the 'reform and overhaul CARB' language and explicit LCFS credit-price ceiling proposal, but he is not calling to repeal LCFS outright — his gas plan accepts the framework and proposes a price ceiling on compliance costs plus a moratorium on new rules. Stance 2 is the more accurate placement; reviewers should note he sits at the edge of 1-2.

positions.summary: Thurmond would keep refineries operating during the transition while investing in cleaner technology like carbon capture, and offset higher fuel costs for Californians via a tax credit rather than by loosening rules. He has not proposed suspending or weakening LCFS or CARB rules; his framing is 'balance' — continue climate progress while protecting consumers.
positions.source_quote: We can do a better job at balance... We have to find ways to balance climate change, but we also have to invest in technologies like carbon capture that allow refineries to get safer.
positions.notes: Thurmond is described as the most progressive Democrat in the field and has touted shutting down idle oil wells and CalSTRS fossil-fuel divestment, which could argue for stance 4. But on LCFS / refinery emissions rules specifically, the only on-record fuel position is 'balance + carbon capture + tax credits' — i.e., maintain current framework. Mapped to 3 absent an explicit tightening statement.

positions.summary: Hilton's published 'Plan for $3 Gas' commits to cutting the gas excise tax by 50% via procurement and bureaucracy reform, alongside suspending LCFS and refinery rules. In debate and stump appearances he describes this as 'cutting the gas tax in half'; secondary outlets often shorthand his position as a suspension. Either way he is among the field's most aggressive on the tax mechanism itself.
positions.source_quote: Reduce bureaucracy and reform procurement to reduce excise tax by 50%. California charges 60 cents per gallon in excise taxes, but much of this revenue intended to improve roads and transportation infrastructure is wasted in sprawling, costly and cumbersome design and procurement bureaucracy.
positions.notes: The KQED voter guide (2026-05-11) summarizes Hilton's position as 'reduce the gas tax and suspend the state's Low Carbon Fuel Standard.' Most coverage treats Hilton as a suspension proponent, but his campaign issue page is more specific (50% cut via efficiency, not full suspension). Mapped to 1 because the scale's most-cut option captures his directional intent; the 50%-not-100% nuance is flagged here.

positions.summary: Steyer explicitly opposes a gas tax suspension. His pump-price plan instead activates the California Energy Commission's 'maximum gross refining margin' penalty to cap refiner profits and rebate excess to consumers, and blames high prices on Trump's Iran war and Big Oil rather than on the state tax.
positions.source_quote: I will direct the California Energy Commission (CEC) to activate the 'maximum gross refining margin' penalty to establish a legal ceiling on refinery profits, with excess profits returned to Californians as rebates.
positions.notes: CalMatters 2026-03 article notes Steyer dismissed Mahan and Villaraigosa's gas-tax-style proposals as 'unserious.' At the 2026-04-28 CBS debate, Steyer answered 'no' on suspending the gas tax and pivoted to a windfall profits tax on oil companies. No verbatim signal that he would raise the tax, so mapped to 3 (hold).

positions.summary: Bianco has been the most categorical candidate on eliminating the gas tax outright, framing it as wasted revenue that can be replaced by cutting government waste. He repeats the line in stump speeches, debates, and campaign video.
positions.source_quote: When I'm governor the gas tax is gone. California doesn't need a gas tax to fund roads, it needs to cut the waste, fraud and abuse.
positions.notes: Bianco's campaign-site Affordability & Taxes page does not name the excise tax specifically, but his social posts, KQED voter-guide summary ('eliminating the state's 61-cent-per-gallon gas tax, which funds road repair and transit'), and Riverside County stump events do. High confidence, stance 1.

positions.summary: Becerra is on record opposing a gas tax cut, arguing that the tax funds the roads, bridges, and transit voters use every day. He directs his pump-price answer at supply stability and at Trump-era oil-price spikes rather than at the state tax.
positions.source_quote: [I am] not in favor of cutting the gas tax. ... You have to fund [the roads] somehow. ... I want everyone who is sitting here to drive on the roads, cross our bridges, make sure transit is working.
positions.notes: Multiple debate recaps (CBS, KQED, Streetsblog CA) align that Becerra rejected a suspension at the 2026-04-28 debate. The LAist 2026-04-15 transcript shows the same posture: stabilize supply, not cut the tax. Stance 3 (hold) is solid.

positions.summary: Porter has long opposed raising the gas tax (she voted-with-her-feet against the 2017 SB 1 hike rhetorically) and argues infrastructure should come from the general fund, not from a regressive pump tax. But at the 2026 debate she declined to commit to a temporary suspension, calling rivals' proposals too narrow.
positions.source_quote: I opposed the gas tax increase in 2018. Some of you might not know that 'cause every other Democrat just said sure. ... We do have to, I think, stop imposing gas taxes as a way of funding our infrastructure. Infrastructure benefits all of us. And we should fund it out of the general fund.
positions.notes: Mapped to 2 (pause scheduled increases) rather than 1 because in 2026 Porter has not endorsed an outright suspension and has not put a gas-tax cut on her priorities page; her stated framing is structural — fund infrastructure from the general fund — rather than a current-rate suspension. Daily Wire (2026-04-29) reports her debate answer to a suspension question as 'no.' Could be argued as 3 if one weights the 2026 debate posture over the 2017/2018 voting record; 2 is the directional middle.

positions.summary: Mahan is the highest-profile Democratic candidate calling for an outright temporary suspension of the gas excise tax, with a dedicated /gas-tax page on his campaign site and a debate-stage line that it is 'the most regressive tax in California.' He says he would backfill road funding from elsewhere in the budget.
positions.source_quote: Sacramento has the power to give working Californians real, immediate relief at the pump. A temporary gas tax suspension isn't a political statement — it's a common-sense solution for working families, and I'm willing to fight for it, even if that means standing up to the status quo.
positions.notes: The 2026-04-28 CBS debate line — 'It is the most regressive tax in California. Working people, rural people are spending three times as much maintaining our roads as wealthy EV owners' — has been widely re-reported. Mahan has paired the suspension call with a proposed EV/road-usage charge to broaden the funding base over time. Unambiguous stance 1.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa rejects a gas tax suspension in favor of a price-trigger rebate: when gas crosses $5.50/gallon, the state would return cap-and-invest revenue to drivers. His pump-price agenda focuses on refinery regulations and CARB reform, not on cutting the excise tax itself.
positions.source_quote: Not break the gas tax, but in fact, I said that on your show — a rebate after $5.50.
positions.notes: Villaraigosa is sometimes lumped in with Mahan as a 'suspension Democrat' (e.g., the Legal Insurrection 2026-04-14 piece) but the underlying source is about a regulatory moratorium, not a tax suspension; the LAist transcript explicitly disclaims 'not break the gas tax.' His /gas issues page does not propose changing the excise tax. Confidently 3 (hold) — with a rebate mechanism layered on top.

positions.summary: Thurmond's affordability platform calls for a temporary pause of the state gas tax, framed as relief from 'Trump's Iran War tax,' alongside a working- and middle-class tax credit. He affirmed this position with a 'yes' on suspension at the 2026 CBS California debate.
positions.source_quote: Pause California's Gas tax to provide relief in the midst of Trump's Iran War tax.
positions.notes: Daily Wire (2026-04-29) and CBS Los Angeles debate recap both report Thurmond aligning with Republicans Bianco and Hilton plus Democrat Mahan in supporting a suspension, against Becerra/Porter/Steyer/Villaraigosa who opposed. The campaign-site language is 'pause' — temporary — so stance 1 (suspend) is appropriate; this is not a permanent repeal proposal.

positions.summary: Opposes any changes to Prop 13, including for commercial property. Endorsed by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association PAC (the leading Prop 13 defense organization).
positions.source_quote: I'm proud to have the endorsement of the HJTA PAC. As governor, I'll cut taxes for working people and protect Prop 13 so families can stay in their homes, without property taxes spiraling out of control.
positions.notes: HJTA endorsement is the single strongest signal a candidate can send on Prop 13 — HJTA exists specifically to defend Prop 13. KQED's tax-comparison piece (2026-04-14) confirms: 'He opposed any changes to Proposition 13 and wants to eliminate the minimum franchise tax.' Stance 1 (strengthen) rather than 2 (hold) is appropriate because the HJTA-aligned posture is actively defensive.

positions.summary: Centerpiece campaign proposal: remove Prop 13 protections from commercial and industrial property and reassess them at market value. Has floated a 2027 special election to put it on the ballot. Frames it as closing a 'Trump tax loophole' that benefits wealthy corporate landlords.
positions.source_quote: We need to fund our schools, and I'll do that by changing Prop 13 so that corporations pay real estate taxes based on their property's true value, not its value from the 1970s.
positions.notes: Steyer's own campaign site (tax-loopholes page) explicitly calls to 'reform the commercial side of Prop. 13 to end this corporate tax break that lets the wealthiest property owners, like Donald Trump, avoid paying taxes based on what their skyscrapers, golf courses, and tech campuses are actually worth.' He was a major backer of Prop 15 in 2020 (which failed 52-48), and this 2026 proposal is essentially Prop 15 revisited. Stance 5 (full commercial split-roll, market-value reassessment) rather than 4 (phase-in) because his framing is full assessment, not gradual.

positions.summary: Broadly opposes any new taxes on Californians and businesses, including commercial property tax increases. Has not made explicit Prop 13 protection a campaign theme the way Hilton has, but as a Republican running on eliminating the state income tax, he would clearly oppose split-roll.
positions.source_quote: Californians deserve to keep more of their hard-earned money.
positions.notes: Bianco's campaign-issues page is silent on Prop 13 specifically, but his platform of eliminating the state income tax and opposing any new taxes places him firmly in the anti-split-roll camp. Stance 2 (hold) rather than 1 (strengthen) because, unlike Hilton, he has not made Prop 13 defense an active campaign plank — he simply opposes the tax increase. Source quote is from his affordability/taxes page rather than a Prop 13 statement. Source date is approximate (campaign page, no clear timestamp).

positions.summary: Has not publicly taken a 2026 position on commercial Prop 13 / split-roll. His campaign housing plan and economy/affordability plan make no mention of Prop 13, commercial property tax, or industrial property reassessment. As CA Attorney General he wrote the official Prop 15 (2020) ballot title and summary, but that role was procedural.
positions.notes: Important correction to the context-bundle peer note: the California YIMBY blog (2026-05-12) — the only source for the 'million homes + end Prop 13 for industrial/commercial' framing — actually attributes that revenue plan to STEYER, not Becerra. Multiple WebFetch passes of becerra2026.com/priorities/housing/ and /economy-and-affordability/ found zero Prop 13 / commercial / industrial / property-tax language. KQED's 2026-04-14 tax-comparison story (the canonical 2026-race tax overview) and LAist's parallel piece do not mention Becerra in the commercial-property-tax section at all. The Mission Local recap of the Ezra Klein housing forum (2026-05-08) reports Becerra blamed Trump tariffs and red tape for construction costs, not Prop 13. As AG (2019-2020) Becerra wrote the Prop 15 ballot title — opponents (HJTA) sued, accusing him of biased pro-split-roll wording, but the court ruled the title was not misleading; the wording role is statutorily assigned to the AG's office and not a personal endorsement of split-roll. Without a 2026 campaign statement, the responsible code is 'unknown'. Confidence: insufficient_data.

positions.summary: Has not publicly taken a 2026 position on commercial Prop 13 / split-roll. Her tax plan is built around eliminating state income tax for households under $100k and raising the state corporate income tax from a flat 8.84% to a progressive scale topping out at 9.75% — explicitly different levers than commercial property tax.
positions.notes: Both of Porter's tax-relevant priority pages (Fighting Income Inequality, Lowering Housing Costs) describe only the corporate income tax and personal income tax — no Prop 13, no commercial property tax, no split-roll language. KQED's 2026-04-09 Political Breakdown episode and KQED's 2026-04-14 candidate tax-comparison piece confirm her platform stops at corporate income tax. The SF Examiner story on Steyer's 2027 special-election split-roll plan (the canonical 'who-supports-split-roll-in-the-2026-race' inventory) names only Betty Yee as a Democratic rival of Steyer's expressing support 'in concept,' and reports Mahan and Villaraigosa as opposed; Porter is conspicuously absent from both lists. Given the political toxicity of split-roll after Prop 15's 2020 defeat and Porter's deliberately moderate-tax messaging (income-tax cut for the middle class), her silence reads as a deliberate non-endorsement rather than a mere oversight. Coding 'unknown' is the responsible call; if forced to guess, a 2 (hold) is more likely than a 4-5 given her platform's structure, but inferring without a quote is inappropriate. Confidence: insufficient_data.

positions.summary: Opposes raising taxes — including commercial property taxes — until state government demonstrates better spending oversight. Has explicitly opposed Steyer's split-roll proposal.
positions.source_quote: We need to make government work better before we ask families and small businesses to pay more.
positions.notes: Mahan responded specifically to Steyer's split-roll proposal with the quoted statement, framing it as small-business protection. Steyer escalated the dispute on X, accusing Mahan of protecting 'billionaires and MAGA donors.' KQED confirms Mahan 'vows to oppose all tax increases until oversight measures are in place.' Stance 2 (hold) rather than 1 (strengthen) because his framing is fiscal-discipline / oversight rather than Prop 13 defense as a principle.

positions.summary: Opposes Steyer's split-roll proposal in the 2026 race, citing the 2020 Prop 15 defeat as evidence voters have already decided the issue. His campaign site commits to 'holding the line on property taxes' generally. Notable reversal from his 2017 statements as LA mayor when he advocated split-roll.
positions.source_quote: A rushed, off-year special election in 2027 to raise corporate taxes isn't serious governing; it's an expensive political gamble.
positions.notes: Important reversal: in 2017, as a previous gubernatorial candidate, Villaraigosa advocated for split-roll in a Sacramento Press Club speech and told reporters 'all aspects of Proposition 13 should be reviewed.' In 2026 he is running with the State Building & Construction Trades Council backing but has shifted to a defensive position, likely reflecting the post-Prop-15 political environment and his Latino-business / moderate-coalition strategy. His campaign plan section is titled 'A Commitment to Hold the Line on Taxes' and reads: 'Holding the line on property taxes is about protecting working- and middle-class families, keeping seniors in their homes, and making sure Californians are not pushed out of an already expensive market.' Stance 2 (hold) rather than 1 because his framing is housing-affordability not Prop 13 sanctity, and the 2017 history means he's not a doctrinaire Prop 13 defender.

positions.summary: Explicitly supports closing Prop 13 'loopholes for corporations' while protecting homeowners, seniors, and small businesses — a clear commercial split-roll position. Reinforces his 2020 endorsement of Proposition 15 (the failed commercial split-roll initiative), which he supported as Superintendent of Public Instruction alongside Sen. Kamala Harris as the only statewide officials backing it.
positions.source_quote: I think we tax billionaires and closed loopholes for corporations like in Prop 13. That won't mean any new taxes for seniors or for homeowners, or for small businesses.
positions.notes: Direct quote from KQED's Political Breakdown podcast/PBS broadcast — interview recorded 2026-03-17, aired on PBS 2026-03-26. The quote pairs closing 'loopholes for corporations like in Prop 13' with an explicit carve-out for seniors, homeowners, and small businesses — which is precisely the structure of a commercial split-roll (Prop 15 was titled to leave residential and small commercial alone). Coupled with his 2020 Prop 15 endorsement (he was one of only two statewide officials backing it; the other was then-Senator Harris), this is the most overtly pro-split-roll position of any 2026 gubernatorial candidate after Steyer. Coding 5 (full commercial split-roll — tax commercial at market value) rather than 4 (phased) because (a) the rhetoric is unhedged ('close the loophole') rather than incremental, (b) his 2020 endorsement was for a non-phased measure that reassessed all qualifying commercial/industrial at market value with a small-business carve-out, and (c) no public statement suggests he favors a more gradual approach. The boundary between 4 and 5 is admittedly narrow here — Steyer's centerpiece special-election proposal is coded 5 and Thurmond's rhetoric matches Steyer's, so consistency favors 5. Confidence: high (verbatim quote, primary source, dated, and consistent with prior endorsement record).

positions.summary: Hilton makes Prop 13 a core campaign pillar — 'Protect Prop. 13!' appears explicitly in his tax platform alongside a commitment to no property tax increases. He frames any reform attempt (including split-roll) as part of the affordability problem and is the most vocal defender of Prop 13 in the field.
positions.source_quote: No increase in property taxes. Protect Prop.13!
positions.notes: Stance 1 (strengthen) rather than 2 (hold) because Hilton uses Prop 13 as an affirmative pillar of his economic message — KQED reports he 'opposed any changes to Proposition 13' and he uses Prop 13 defense to argue for cutting related fees (impact fees) as well. He is positioning himself to capture Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association-aligned voters.

positions.summary: Steyer is the most aggressive Prop 13 reformer in the field on COMMERCIAL property — vowing a 2027 special election to close what he calls the 'corporate real estate tax loophole' — but is explicit that residential Prop 13 protections stay intact. On the residential question specifically, his stance is hold-the-line.
positions.source_quote: Steyer wants to retain Prop 13 for residential property, but repeal its benefits for commercial property, which he has called a 'corporate tax loophole' that costs the state $20 billion per year.
positions.notes: Important framing: on the COMMERCIAL Prop 13 question (a separate issue), Steyer would be stance 5. On the RESIDENTIAL question scored here, he is explicitly stance 2 — he has gone out of his way to wall off residential protections from his reform pitch, calling Prop 13 untouchable for homeowners. This is the cleanest illustration of why split-roll proponents register as stance 2 on this specific issue.

positions.summary: Bianco has not made Prop 13 a focal point of his campaign but is a hard-line tax-cutter (proposes eliminating the state income tax) and Riverside County's Republican sheriff aligned with Howard Jarvis-style tax-defense politics. His tax platform opposes all new taxes; no reporting suggests any opening to residential Prop 13 reform.
positions.source_quote: Californians deserve to keep more of their hard-earned money.
positions.notes: Bianco's affordability/taxes page does not mention Prop 13 by name, so the source quote is the closest direct quote from his own platform. Coded stance 1 (strengthen) rather than 2 (hold) by reasonable inference: he is a Republican county sheriff running on aggressive tax cuts and would be expected to align with the Save Prop 13 November 2026 ballot initiative if asked. Confidence is medium rather than high because he has not affirmatively addressed Prop 13 himself in 2026 coverage we surveyed.

positions.summary: Has not publicly taken a 2026 position on residential Proposition 13. His campaign housing plan and economy/affordability plan make no mention of Prop 13, residential property tax, or any inheritance/transfer-rule reform. As CA Attorney General he wrote the official Prop 15 (2020) ballot title and summary, but that role was procedural and not a personal endorsement; Prop 15 in any case targeted only commercial/industrial property and would not have changed residential rules.
positions.notes: CORRECTION: this entry overrides a previous coding of stance 2 that relied on a misattributed quote from the California YIMBY blog (cayimby.org, 2026-05-12). On verification, the blog's 'million homes paired with a revenue plan of ending Proposition 13 protections for industrial and commercial property' framing actually appears in the Tom Steyer section of the post, not the Becerra section — the Becerra section only mentions his AG-era housing-law enforcement, the Coastal Commission directive, the 90-day permit rule, and an insurance-rate freeze. Becerra's own campaign pages on housing and economy/affordability contain zero Prop 13 / property-tax language. KQED's 2026-04-14 tax-comparison piece and LAist's parallel piece do not attribute any Prop 13 position to him either. Without a 2026 statement, the responsible code is 'unknown' / insufficient_data, matching the prop13_commercial coding for Becerra. Adjacent values considered: stance 2 (hold) remains the field-consensus soft inference, but the previous stance-2 coding cited evidence that does not exist as written, so the honest call is to downgrade rather than substitute new inference for the missing quote.

positions.summary: Porter has not published a position on residential Proposition 13. Her gubernatorial tax platform is built entirely around income tax (eliminating it for households under $100,000) and a progressive corporate tax (replacing the flat 8.84% rate with a graduated structure topping out near 9.75%), and she has been conspicuously silent on Prop 13, residential property tax, split-roll, and Prop 19 transfer/inheritance reform across her campaign site, 2026 debate appearances, KQED town hall, and major media coverage. Soft inference from the field consensus (every other surveyed Democrat lands at stance 2, hold residential protections) and from her income/corporate-tax revenue focus would point to stance 2, but she has not personally endorsed even that posture in any sourced statement.
positions.source_quote: California's economy is the 4th largest in the world. Yet our tax structure treats a local small business turning a single dollar in profit the same as a global corporation that brings in billions in profits. We have a flat corporate tax, and that must change. As Governor, I will launch a Progressive Corporate Tax.
positions.notes: The source_quote above is from Porter's own tax-platform page and is used because the verifiable, citable fact is the documented absence of a Prop 13 / property-tax mechanism in her revenue plan — her stated revenue source is the progressive corporate tax, not property-tax reform. This contrasts directly with Steyer (commercial split-roll, stance 2 residential but 5 commercial) and Thurmond (explicit homeowner/senior wall against any Prop 13 change). Porter's silence is notable precisely because the housing-cost framing she leads with — a single mom whose teenagers won't be able to buy houses in California — is the exact emotional terrain where a reform-leaning candidate (Prop 19 inheritance-loophole closure, transfer-rule tweaks at stance 3) might plant a flag, and she has not done so. Considered and ruled out as evidence: (a) iSideWith-style aggregators are not primary sources and were not citable; (b) her 2020 House-incumbent endorsement record on Prop 15 did not surface in Ballotpedia search returns I could verify; (c) her House voting record (2019–2024) is federal and would not directly resolve a California Prop 13 stance even if a related vote surfaced. Honest finding: insufficient data. Adjacent values considered: stance 2 (hold) is the most likely soft inference given field consensus and her revenue strategy not touching residential property tax, but it requires an inference rather than a quote; stance 1 (strengthen) is unlikely given she has not aligned rhetorically with Howard Jarvis-style tax-defense politics; stances 3–5 (any residential reform) are unlikely given she has had multiple debate and platform opportunities to plant such a flag and has not.

positions.summary: Mahan opposes Steyer's commercial split-roll proposal and has staked out a no-new-taxes posture pending efficiency reforms. He has not called for any reform to Prop 13, residential or commercial — he is positioning as the tech-backed moderate defending the status quo on property taxation.
positions.source_quote: We need to make government work better before we ask families and small businesses to pay more.
positions.notes: Mahan's only documented engagement with Prop 13 in 2026 is his rejection of Steyer's commercial split-roll proposal — Steyer publicly attacked him on X for 'want[ing] to preserve this egregious corporate property tax loophole.' Mahan has not addressed RESIDENTIAL Prop 13 directly, but a candidate defending commercial Prop 13 against split-roll is plainly stance 2 (or stronger) on the residential question by implication. Coded stance 2 rather than 1 because his framing is 'fix government first, then talk taxes,' not active Prop 13 defense like Hilton's.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa's 2026 position is muddled but lands on defending homeowner property taxes. He said at a debate he'd 'fix' Prop 13 while also 'holding the line on property taxes,' and has publicly opposed Steyer's 2027 special-election split-roll plan as 'an expensive political gamble' — siding with status quo on the residential question.
positions.source_quote: Early in the evening, Villaraigosa said he rejected Prop 13 — a 1970s era policy that caps property tax increases across the state — but wanted to 'hold the line on property taxes.' He later said he wanted to 'fix' Prop 13 but didn't clarify how he could accomplish it while holding the line on property taxes.
positions.notes: Villaraigosa was an early advocate (as LA mayor, c. 2009-2012) for revisiting Prop 13 on commercial property. In 2026 he has dialed that back: explicit opposition to Steyer's 2027 special election, and the debate quote above shows him defending residential homeowner tax stability. Stance 2 (hold residential) with low-medium confidence because his 'fix Prop 13' language hints he could be open to limited reforms (stance 3) — but he has not specified what 'fix' means and has paired it with the homeowner-protection caveat.

positions.summary: Thurmond endorsed Prop 15 in 2020 (commercial split-roll) and has reiterated in 2026 that closing 'Prop 13 loopholes' should target corporations, not homeowners. His direct quote walls off seniors, homeowners, and small businesses from any tax change. On residential Prop 13 specifically, this is a hold-the-line stance.
positions.source_quote: I think we tax billionaires and close loopholes for corporations like in Prop 13. That won't mean any new taxes for seniors or for homeowners, or for small businesses.
positions.notes: Like Steyer and Becerra, Thurmond is a split-roll supporter (stance 5 on a commercial Prop 13 question) who scores stance 2 here because residential protections are explicitly preserved. The Oakland Voices interview quote is the cleanest direct statement we have from him distinguishing homeowner from corporate treatment. Confidence is medium pending a second corroborating quote from a major outlet — his 2026 messaging has emphasized a billionaire wealth tax more than Prop 13 reform.

positions.summary: Hilton would eliminate state income tax entirely for Californians earning under $100,000 and replace the current graduated brackets with a flat 7.5% rate on income above $100,000. He says this removes ~7.1 million California households (over half) from paying any state income tax, with the cut for $70K-$100K earners (who currently pay rates up to 9.3%) being especially large.
positions.source_quote: If you earn less than $100,000 → you pay no state income tax. ... A single, simple 7.5% rate on income above $100,000.
positions.notes: Stance 1 (significantly cut) is unambiguous. For a household earning $80K, this is a move from ~9.3% marginal / ~5% effective state tax to zero. KQED's round-up describes it as 'eliminating state income tax for Californians earning less than $100,000 and imposing a flat 7.5% tax on earnings over $100,000.' He reiterated the plan on the CNN debate stage May 5, 2026.

positions.summary: Steyer has no proposal to cut or raise middle-income state income tax rates. His revenue plan is built around closing corporate tax loopholes and split-roll commercial property reform to raise ~$20 billion per year, and he supports the November 2026 billionaire wealth tax. He explicitly frames the plan as not adding any new tax on working people.
positions.source_quote: Tom is going to close these corporate loopholes, and raise $20 billion of new revenue each year to fund things like education, healthcare, childcare, and home care, all without charging working people a penny.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (hold) is the cleanest fit: he is silent on middle-income brackets but explicit that working people will not pay more. He has not proposed any middle-income tax credit (which would make him stance 2) — his redistribution flows directly through services funded by corporate/wealth revenue rather than through middle-income tax relief. Distinct from Porter, who proposes both a corporate raise AND a middle-income rate cut.

positions.summary: Bianco's signature pledge is to eliminate California's state income tax entirely — for every income bracket, including the middle — funded by 'wasteful spending' cuts, anti-fraud enforcement, and expanded oil drilling. Middle-income filers would owe $0 in state income tax under his plan.
positions.source_quote: So, as your governor, we will work immediately on eliminating California income tax for all of Californians. ... Other states have done it. There's nine states that don't have a state income tax. So why does the greatest state in the country have an income tax?
positions.notes: Stance 1 (significantly cut) is unambiguous — full elimination is the largest possible middle-income tax cut in the field. KQED's round-up confirms: 'he wants to cut them and make up for lost revenue with undefined wasteful spending cuts.' Bianco frames this as 'Californians deserve to keep more of their hard-earned money' on his campaign site.

positions.summary: Becerra has not proposed any change to California's middle-income state income tax brackets. His tax framing is about raising effective rates on passive income and very-high-wealth filers so they pay at least as much as teachers and firefighters — not about adjusting the brackets that middle earners face. His affordability agenda runs through utility rate freezes and price-gouging enforcement rather than middle-income tax cuts.
positions.source_quote: these billionaires end up paying tax rates that are lower than a teacher or a firefighter. ... We have to start to look at passive income because ... most of the government's revenue is income tax. What we fail to note is that when we tax income, we're only taxing those who get paid by check, by salary. And all that passive income — capital gains and other types of income — is taxed far differently.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (hold) — his proposals are about closing the passive-income gap at the top, not changing middle-income brackets. KQED's voter guide notes he 'favors higher taxes on wealthy individuals but has not proposed a specific income tax plan' for other brackets. Confidence is medium because he hasn't been asked the middle-income question directly and head-on in the sources I found; the inference is from his stated tax philosophy, not from a verbatim 'I will not change middle-income rates' statement.

positions.summary: Porter's headline policy is to eliminate state income tax for Californians making under $100,000, offset by raising California's flat corporate income tax (currently 8.84%) on the highest-earning corporations to up to 9.75% — a change she says would generate up to $8 billion per year. For middle-income filers under $100K, her plan zeroes out state income tax.
positions.source_quote: As Governor, I will work to eliminate state income tax for Californians making under $100,000.
positions.notes: Stance 1 (significantly cut) is unambiguous — zeroing out state income tax for sub-$100K filers is the largest possible cut for the bottom half of middle-income earners. KQED's tax round-up summarizes the plan as 'eliminating state income taxes for families who make under $100,000 ... offset with corporate tax increases.' Distinct from Hilton's same-threshold proposal in that she keeps the existing progressive brackets above $100K intact instead of flattening them.

positions.summary: Mahan has pledged to oppose new tax increases and frames his platform as 'results before more taxes,' but he has not proposed cutting middle-income state income tax rates. His tax-cut proposals are narrow and sectoral — a temporary gas-tax suspension, a two-year tax holiday on new housing construction, and fee caps on infill housing — rather than a change to middle-income brackets.
positions.source_quote: Matt won't ask Californians to pay more in taxes without results.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (hold) is the honest read. LAist's voter-guide one-liner lumped Mahan and Porter together as 'cut income taxes for middle-income earners,' but Mahan's own campaign materials and interview transcripts show no rate-cut proposal — his commitment is 'no new taxes' (i.e., hold) plus narrow sectoral tax holidays for housing and gas. He explicitly opposes the billionaire wealth tax. Confidence medium because of the LAist summary mismatch; the campaign-site quote is the controlling source.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa's tax pitch is a 'Commitment to Hold the Line on Taxes': he would veto multi-billion-dollar tax hikes that 'squeeze middle-class families,' but he has not proposed cutting middle-income state income tax rates. He argues 'we can't tax our way out of our problems' — framing the current 13.3% top rate as already the highest in the nation — but the plan is to prevent raises, not to roll back the existing middle-income brackets.
positions.source_quote: Antonio will veto any reckless multi-billion dollar tax hike that would squeeze middle-class families even further, and instead demand responsible budgeting, smarter spending, and reforms that protect working people from being used as the state's piggy bank. ... Hold the line on taxes so that working- and middle-class families are not forced to pay twice.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (hold) fits exactly. His framing is structurally anti-raise on middle-class families, but he has not proposed cutting current rates; in the LAist transcript he says even the 13.3% top rate should stay 'unless we do a spending plan.' That's a hold posture, not a cut. He has a Speaker-era record of 'tax cuts for middle-class families' but those were one-time historical actions, not part of his 2026 platform.

positions.summary: Thurmond doesn't propose changing middle-income tax rates, but his package would functionally reduce middle-income tax burden: he supports the November 2026 one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax and would direct the proceeds into a new state tax credit specifically for working- and middle-class Californians, giving them more money 'every month' to cover the cost of gas, groceries, and housing.
positions.source_quote: I plan to tax billionaires and to take the proceeds … to provide a tax credit to working and middle-class Californians. ... [The credit would] give working people and middle-class people more money in their pocket every month to pay for the rising cost of gas, groceries, and housing.
positions.notes: Stance 2 (modestly cut) rather than 3 (hold) because the proposed middle-class tax credit is a real, quantifiable reduction in middle-income net tax burden — it just operates through credits rather than rate cuts. Distinguished from Porter/Hilton/Bianco (stance 1) because Thurmond keeps the existing rate structure intact and the credit is one-time/cycle-bound rather than a permanent zeroing-out of a bracket. Distinguished from Steyer (stance 3) because Steyer's revenue plan funds services, not a direct middle-class tax credit.

positions.summary: Hilton's plan is deregulation plus monopoly break-up from the right: repeal the Renewable Portfolio Standard and Renewable Energy Credits, scrap climate mandates he says inflate ratepayer bills, end PG&E's 'state-protected monopoly,' and expand locally owned utilities and rooftop solar so customers can buy elsewhere. He has launched a 'Cal DOGE' proposal to cut state energy regulators directly to lower electricity costs. He promises to roughly halve electricity bills via this combination.
positions.source_quote: California should not be locked into a single, state-protected monopoly utility... Move away from PG&E's monopoly model and toward locally owned utilities... Repeal climate mandates that force utilities into costly energy choices and wasteful spending.
positions.notes: Coded 1 (deregulate) rather than 4 (break up monopolies) because Hilton's primary mechanism is repealing state mandates / RPS / RECs and 'auditing system costs of renewables' — i.e., shrinking the regulatory state — with the anti-monopoly framing serving the same deregulatory goal (open the market). His insurance position is similarly market-restoration: 'The industry needs to be able to take account of future risk, including climate' (Newsweek). Notably right-coded but with a populist anti-PG&E edge.

positions.summary: Steyer wants to lower electricity bills ~25% by structurally constraining investor-owned utilities short of nationalizing them: cut the CPUC-guaranteed ~10% rate of return on capital projects, fill CPUC seats with ratepayer-side commissioners, expand community choice aggregators so cities/counties can form publicly owned power providers, and shift to distributed generation (rooftop solar, batteries, microgrids) so customers have alternatives. On gas, he proposes a refinery profit cap. On insurance, he focuses on home-hardening plus pressure on insurers.
positions.source_quote: We're going to have a different rule at the Public Utilities Commission about how they get paid. And we're going to introduce local competition... Households shouldn't be forced to pay more so that utilities can earn a guaranteed 10 percent return on their investments... stop the utilities from acting like monopolies and build a truly distributed, competitive, and resilient energy system.
positions.notes: Stance 4 (public option / break-up monopolies via competition) is the cleanest fit. He explicitly disclaimed nationalization in the CalMatters piece ('not actually arguing for breaking up PG&E') so stance 5 is wrong. But every concrete lever he names — cutting utility rate of return, ending the monopoly framework, enabling municipal/CCA public power — points to weakening IOU market power rather than just stronger CPUC oversight, which separates him from Becerra (stance 3).

positions.summary: Bianco's lever is deregulation across the supply side: lift drilling prohibitions, scrap the 61-cent gas tax, keep Diablo Canyon running, expand nuclear/hydrogen/geothermal under a market-driven framework, and 'hold the CPUC and CEC accountable' for rate hikes — framed as deregulatory accountability rather than rate-freeze intervention. On insurance, he wants to 'stop insurers from leaving California by ensuring a stable and fair regulatory environment' and shore up the FAIR Plan, blaming wildfire / 'failed environmental policy' for insurer flight.
positions.source_quote: Hold the CPUC and CEC accountable for allowing rate price increases to take effect... Unleash the California energy industry by lifting prohibitions and restrictions on new drilling... Stop Insurers from Leaving California by ensuring a stable and fair regulatory environment.
positions.notes: Coded 1 (deregulate) because every proposed lever pulls toward less state intervention: more drilling, less environmental review, less rate-cap regulation on insurance, regulators 'held accountable' for letting rate hikes through rather than empowered to freeze rates. He does not propose breaking up PG&E or creating public utilities.

positions.summary: Becerra's signature affordability proposal is a state-of-emergency freeze on both utility rates and homeowners-insurance premiums while the state investigates the cost drivers, paired with 'stronger oversight and accountability of our utilities.' He pitches it as a temporary intervention — sit everyone down, get behind the curtain, and resume normal rate-setting only after the audit. He does not propose breaking up IOUs or creating a public option; the structural model stays, but with much stronger CPUC oversight and immediate price controls.
positions.source_quote: As Governor, I will freeze utility rates and home insurance premiums. Californians are getting gouged and dropped without explanation. No more. I will fight back for California families.
positions.notes: Textbook stance 3: explicit rate freeze plus CPUC accountability/transparency, no structural break-up, no public takeover. Note the credibility tension flagged by Energy and Policy Institute — Becerra took $153K+ from PG&E/SCE/SDG&E in prior federal/AG races but has not taken utility money in the governor race. The legality of a governor-imposed insurance-rate freeze under Prop 103 / Insurance Commissioner authority was challenged at the April debate; Becerra argued back. Porter publicly disagreed at the same event, warning a freeze would accelerate insurer departures.

positions.summary: Porter frames utility costs as a consumer-protection problem and has said the CPUC 'is no longer fighting' for Californians and 'needs to have a reboot and a refresh.' In Congress she co-led opposition to CPUC's proposed monthly fixed charge on electric bills regardless of usage. On insurance, she publicly opposed a Becerra-style rate freeze, warning insurers would keep leaving, and instead proposes state-dollar interventions to bring costs down. No proposal to break up PG&E or create a public option.
positions.source_quote: Many Californians feel like the Public Utilities Commission is no longer fighting for them... The Public Utilities Commission needs to have a reboot and a refresh.
positions.notes: Coded 3 (rate-side intervention + significant CPUC reform) rather than 4 because she has not endorsed structural break-up, public option, or community-choice expansion as a primary lever, and rejected Becerra's freeze as too blunt on insurance. Her brand is regulator-accountability — pointing-at-the-whiteboard hearings, not breaking up utilities. Confidence medium because her own campaign site doesn't elaborate utility-specific proposals beyond clean-energy investment; the CPUC 'reboot' quote is from a forum, not a written platform document.

positions.summary: Mahan's utility-rate stance centers on cost-shift protection rather than rate freezes or utility break-ups. As San Jose mayor he stepped back from a municipal takeover of PG&E and signed a 2024 partnership giving PG&E performance milestones to serve data centers and other large users for ~$2.5M/year in city revenue. His May 2026 'hold Big Tech accountable' plan elevates this to a campaign centerpiece: require large data centers and major energy users to cover their own surging electrical costs and contribute to renewable-energy and grid infrastructure, rather than shifting costs onto residential ratepayers.
positions.source_quote: A large portion of Mahan's plan focuses on forcing AI and data center companies to cover surging electrical costs and address the environmental impacts on the electrical grid.
positions.notes: Stance unchanged at 2 (modest regulation, grid investment + cost-shift protection). Refreshed from a stale '2024'/low-confidence record to his May 2026 statewide plan, which makes data-center cost-shift protection a campaign centerpiece; confidence raised low->medium. The source quote is the SF Standard's characterization of his unveiled plan, not a verbatim Mahan transcript; the 2024 San Jose PG&E deal remains as corroborating secondary evidence.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa's energy frame is 'all-of-the-above' generation plus grid build-out — renewables, nuclear, natural gas, and faster transmission permitting — paired with a moratorium on new climate regulations he says burden ratepayers. He has not proposed a rate freeze, CPUC structural reform, or a public option. On insurance he focuses on fixing the FAIR Plan rather than capping rates: 'The Fair Plan, which is an unfair plan, not abiding by Prop 103, we got to make it work.'
positions.source_quote: We need an 'All of the Above' energy policy, with renewables like solar and wind, but also nuclear, natural gas, and yes, gas-powered cars... By building our generation capacity, we can meet our energy needs and goals, while creating jobs and ultimately, making energy more affordable.
positions.notes: Coded 2 (modest regulation, grid investment) by inference: his proposed mechanism for lower bills is more supply (build more generation, build transmission faster) plus rolling back climate mandates, not rate-side intervention or structural break-up. Confidence low because his affordability plan and issues page do not contain dedicated utility-rate sections — Fair Plan reform is his most concrete rate-adjacent position.

positions.summary: Thurmond is one of the most interventionist candidates on insurance — he would withhold state tax credits, subsidies, and benefits from insurers that refuse to write policies, and would restrict rate increases unless insurers maintain coverage. On electricity/utility rates specifically, his platform foregrounds clean-energy jobs and broad affordability rather than CPUC structural reform or a public option; he has not endorsed breaking up PG&E or creating a state utility, but he frames the cost crisis as one the state must use leverage to fix.
positions.source_quote: The state should restrict rate increases unless insurers continue offering coverage... [Thurmond] would withhold tax credits, subsidies and benefits from noncooperative insurers.
positions.notes: Coded 3 (rate-side intervention + CPUC reform-coded) by combining (a) his explicit willingness to use state coercion to restrict insurance rate hikes with (b) the absence of any public-option / break-up / state-takeover language. He is to the left of Mahan/Villaraigosa on rate intervention (because of the insurer-leverage proposal) but to the right of Steyer on structural reform. Confidence medium rather than high because he has issued no dedicated electricity-rate or CPUC platform, and the legality of his insurer-coercion tactic was questioned by debate moderators.

positions.summary: Hilton frames public safety as the foundation of his platform: enforce existing laws, fully support officers, back Prop 36, and crack down across the board on homelessness, drugs, theft, illegal immigration, and violent crime. His pitch is consistent enforcement without new reform; he cites violent crime up 23% and arrest rates falling to 30% statewide as proof the current system is failing.
positions.source_quote: We need to get back to the basic principle that we should enforce the law... As governor, I will ensure our brave law enforcement officers are fully supported in enforcing the law.
positions.notes: Stance 1 (rather than 2) because Hilton's framing is enforcement-only with zero rhetorical concession to reform, oversight, or non-police alternatives. He explicitly cites Prop 36 support and the need for prosecutions/convictions; the platform does not mention accountability, body cameras, oversight commissions, or non-police responders. ACLU CA Action survey shows he declined to engage on civil-liberties/oversight questions, which is consistent with a stance-1 placement.

positions.summary: Steyer self-describes as a progressive criminal-justice reformer: incarcerate violent people, but rehabilitate and treat nonviolent offenders rather than imprison them. He highlights his role in passing SB 10 (eliminating cash bail as a precondition for release) and frames ICE as a criminal organization he would prosecute. He has not been a vocal champion of expanded police hiring.
positions.source_quote: Steyer is a big believer in keeping communities safe and incarcerating violent people who are a danger, but for nonviolent criminals, he believes rehabilitating and treating them is a much more successful and effective way to deal with crime.
positions.notes: Stance 4 rather than 3 or 5: Steyer's criminal-justice page is framed as reform-and-rehabilitation, his major proud point is bail reform (SB 10), and he has not proposed expanding police hiring; but he also explicitly endorses incarcerating violent offenders, which keeps him short of stance 5 (substantial divestment from policing). He did not respond to the ACLU CA Action survey, which limits confidence vs. the other Democrats. His ICE-prosecution rhetoric is the loudest law-enforcement plank, but that targets federal agents, not California policing.

positions.summary: A sitting Riverside County sheriff with PORAC's endorsement, Bianco runs on the most explicitly tough-on-crime platform in the field: roll back Prop 47's $950 felony threshold, restore cash bail for serious and violent offenses, end DA non-prosecution policies, expand the Retail Crime Task Force, build on Prop 36's penalty increases, and 'stand behind the line officers who have been sued, scapegoated, and second-guessed.'
positions.source_quote: roll back Prop 47's $950 felony threshold, restore cash bail for serious and violent offenses... end DA non-prosecution policies through statewide accountability standards... stand behind the line officers who have been sued, scapegoated, and second-guessed for the better part of a decade.
positions.notes: Stance 1 is the textbook fit. Bianco is a sitting sheriff, has been the loudest opponent of Prop 47 and zero-bail, and was endorsed by PORAC. The 2023 CA DOJ investigation of his department for alleged unconstitutional policing/excessive-force/jail-conditions issues underscores the absence of any reform plank in his platform — he frames officer 'accountability' demands as the problem to be reversed, not embraced.

positions.summary: Becerra threads the needle: 'tough on people who are committing crime' while also focused on getting them 'off the path of committing crime' through mental-health, addiction, and reentry services. As CA AG he pushed Congress to give state AGs federal authority to investigate patterns of unconstitutional policing; CalMatters previously noted he was less aggressive than progressives wanted on disclosing police misconduct records.
positions.source_quote: We want to make sure we're tough on people who are committing crime, but we also want to make sure that we can get them off the path of committing crime... If we don't provide the services that you need, whether it's mental health, drug addiction services... let's do what we know works, provide people with the services that let them rehabilitate and get on the right path.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (mixed) fits because Becerra explicitly couples 'tough' enforcement with rehabilitation/services and has a record of pushing federal pattern-or-practice authority — but he is not a stance-4 reformer (CalMatters reporting from his AG tenure flagged him as cautious on police-record disclosure and SB 1421 implementation). He answered 'yes' to the ACLU CA Action 2026 survey questions on community alternatives and oversight, which prevents drift to stance 2. Note: his campaign site has NO dedicated public-safety/policing page — these positions come from interviews and his AG record, which lowers confidence.

positions.summary: Porter explicitly endorses criminal-justice reform: revisit three-strikes, look at compassionate/hospice release for elderly long-sentenced inmates, and acknowledge that Prop 36 is 'focused on punishment' — 'we need punishment, but we really need to dig in on prevention.' Her campaign has no standalone public-safety page; policing is not a major emphasis.
positions.source_quote: We're definitely moving in the right direction on criminal justice reform, particularly in terms of looking back at what are the consequences of our three strike law... We've passed Prop 36, that's focused on punishment. We need punishment, but we really need to dig in on prevention and making our streets feel safe.
positions.notes: Stance 4 because Porter's ABC10 framing is prevention-first, she's actively critiquing three-strikes and Prop 36's punishment posture, and she answered 'yes' across the ACLU CA Action survey to oversight/community-alternatives questions. She has not proposed expanded police hiring (unlike Mahan, Villaraigosa, Thurmond). Confidence is medium not high because policing is conspicuously absent from her 12-priority list on katieporter.com — her brand is consumer protection, not criminal justice — so we are inferring from one ABC10 interview plus the ACLU survey.

positions.summary: Mahan's gubernatorial pitch is 'community policing and hired more officers — helping make San Jose the safest big city in America,' anchored by his San Jose record: doubled SJPD hiring to 30+ officers/year, plans 200 new sworn + 100 community service officers, deployed Automatic License Plate Readers, was a 'main proponent' of Prop 36 in 2024, and paired the expansion with a new Independent Police Auditor and accountability dashboards.
positions.source_quote: Matt believes there are two sure-fire ways to keep crime low: assure consequences and build trust. People now know, if they harm San Jose, they will be found and held accountable. They also know their neighborhood police officer.
positions.notes: Stance 2 (expand law enforcement with modest reforms) is the right read. Governance-vs-rhetoric note: campaign messaging is 'common sense' and trust-building, but the governing actions are unambiguously expansionary — doubled SJPD hiring, ALPRs (which civil-liberties groups sued San Jose over), and Prop 36 endorsement. He cannot be coded stance 1 because he did appoint an Independent Police Auditor and built accountability dashboards into the program. He cannot be coded stance 3 because his rhetoric is not 'more accountability AND more officers in equal measure' — accountability is a supporting beam, not a co-equal pillar. Mahan did not respond to the ACLU CA Action 2026 survey, which is itself a signal he doesn't want to lock in progressive policing commitments.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa runs on his LA mayoral public-safety record: hired ~1,000 new LAPD officers (force exceeded 10,000 for the first time), violent crime down 48%, federally-modeled gang intervention programs, and the end of the LAPD federal consent decree. He explicitly supported Prop 36 and frames himself as the only Democrat with both law-enforcement and reform credibility — PORAC endorsed him (along with Bianco) in 2025.
positions.source_quote: I led the fight against 'three strikes, you're out' when I was in the legislature. I'm against the death penalty, but I tell people I believe in accountability. When you keep on stealing and you're on drugs and you get arrested and you refuse drug treatment the first time, the second time, the third time, you're going to jail. That's why I supported Prop 36.
positions.notes: Stance 2 (expand law enforcement with modest reforms). Governance-vs-rhetoric gap: his 1990s legislative record fighting three-strikes would suggest stance 3-4, but his 2026 campaign explicitly leads with +1,000 LAPD officers, Prop 36 endorsement, and PORAC's endorsement — code to the current platform, not the 30-year-old legislative votes. He is not stance 1 because he did oversee the end of LAPD's federal consent decree by satisfying its reform terms, ran community/gang intervention programs, and answered 'yes' to ACLU CA Action's oversight/community-alternatives questions. PORAC's dual endorsement with Bianco is a strong signal of his current law-enforcement-supportive positioning.

positions.summary: Thurmond explicitly rejects a 'police your way out' approach and pairs his proposal to hire thousands more officers and increase 911 dispatch capacity with crime intervention, job-training programs, mental health, and substance-use treatment. He frames police accountability and community programs as co-equal pillars, drawing on his Richmond city council record.
positions.source_quote: The only way we're going to really address crime issues is to have a combination of police officers who are accountable to the community and intervention programs that create job opportunities. I don't think we can police our way out of all the challenges.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (mixed) fits cleanly. He explicitly proposes both expanded hiring (thousands of officers + 911 dispatch) AND accountability + intervention as co-equal pillars — the textbook stance-3 framing. ACLU CA Action survey confirms 'yes' across community-alternatives, social-service responders, oversight, and facial-recognition-ban questions. He is not stance 4 because his plan visibly includes a major expansion in police hiring; not stance 2 because intervention and accountability are positioned as co-equal, not bolt-ons.

positions.summary: Hilton attacks Prop 47 directly on his campaign homepage as having effectively legalized theft under $950, and frames Prop 36 as a partial fix that Newsom is starving of resources. He pairs this with calls to expand prison capacity and 'enforce the law,' placing him among the candidates most aggressive on rolling back Prop 47.
positions.source_quote: Now that Proposition 36, which Democrats like Gavin Newsom fought so strongly, has passed, it's amazing to think that anyone ever thought it was a good idea to make theft under $950 a day legal.
positions.notes: Stance 1 is supported by his explicit attack on Prop 47 (the $950 threshold) and the broader 'enforce the law' framing on theft, drugs, homelessness, and immigration. CalMatters' May 2026 round-up attributes the 'Prop 36 could have solved a lot of the state's problems but Newsom won't fund it' framing to Bianco, not Hilton, so I am NOT relying on that quote for Hilton's stance.

positions.summary: Steyer accepts Prop 36 as the people's will and frames it primarily as a treatment-over-incarceration measure that the state has failed to fund. He emphasizes rehabilitation, not further rollback of Prop 47, and his broader criminal-justice messaging is critical of California's history of 'mass incarceration.'
positions.source_quote: We need treatment, not incarceration, where it's available.
positions.notes: Steyer's campaign Issues page does not have a dedicated public-safety or Prop 36 sub-page, so the primary verbatim quote is from the KTVU Feb 3 2026 statewide gubernatorial debate. He has publicly accepted Prop 36 as voter-approved policy and pushed for fuller funding rather than rollback. Stance 3 (implement as passed) is the cleanest fit; he is not advocating to further toughen, nor explicitly to narrow.

positions.summary: As a Republican sheriff who campaigned for Prop 36, Bianco wants to go further: fully reverse Prop 47, build off Prop 36 with additional penalty restorations, and expand the Retail Crime Task Force. Public safety is the explicit top plank of his campaign.
positions.source_quote: I am going to ensure that crime is actually a crime again. We cannot have a civilized California with people who are victimizing us over and over and over again.
positions.notes: Stance 1 confirmed by multiple sources: his Public Safety platform explicitly commits to 'build off the success of Prop 36 by continuing to restore penalties for serious crimes' and CalMatters' May 2026 piece reports he wants to 'fully reverse Prop 47.' He also said in the July 31 2024 Fox 11 debate that Prop 47 was 'the beginning of the end for public safety in California.' Highest-confidence stance in the field.

positions.summary: Becerra accepts the 68% voter mandate for Prop 36 and emphasizes that the state must fund the treatment side of the law. He pairs that with explicit skepticism of mass incarceration, citing the over-reach of three-strikes — putting him firmly in the 'implement as passed, fund the treatment' camp.
positions.source_quote: It's a hollow gesture to pass Prop 36 and not provide the funding for mental health services, drug addiction services... Californians are done with just putting people away behind bars. We'd rather have folks who are rehabilitated or who are provided the services they need to stand up again.
positions.notes: Becerra's campaign Issues/Priorities page does not directly address Prop 36/47, so the primary verbatim is the March 3 2026 KQED Political Breakdown interview (hosted on PBS). His three-strikes critique ('going way too far') signals he is not interested in toughening further; his explicit support for Prop 36 implementation rules out stance 4. Stance 3 is the clean fit.

positions.summary: Porter voted yes on Prop 36 in November 2024 despite calling it 'flawed.' She supports the retail-theft penalties but has explicit reservations about the drug-possession side, arguing incarceration for substance use is costly and doesn't 'heal people' — positioning her as an implement-it-but-emphasize-prevention candidate.
positions.source_quote: I support the increased penalties for retail crimes, that's a problem here... The drug substance use part of this, we know that incarcerating people for substance use is incredibly expensive to taxpayers and doesn't actually heal people.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (not 4) because she voted yes and supports the retail-theft component, while her drug-side caveat is a critique of approach rather than a call to narrow Prop 36 implementation. Her campaign Priorities page does not have a public safety section, which limits the source set; the November 2024 CNN interview captured by Politico/Yahoo is the strongest verbatim available. Reconsider stance 4 if her campaign issues a more explicit narrow-implementation position.

positions.summary: Mahan is the loudest Democratic advocate for Prop 36 implementation and the most direct critic of Newsom's $100M funding allocation. He hosts a dedicated Prop 36 plan on his campaign site, frames the law as 'the era of mass treatment,' and wants to close 'repeat offender loopholes' — a tougher-than-stance-3 posture that nonetheless leans on treatment, not pure penalty escalation.
positions.source_quote: Nearly 70% of Californians supported Proposition 36 — not because they wanted to return to an era of mass incarceration, but rather because they knew we needed to start the era of mass treatment.
positions.notes: Stance 2 (not 3) because Mahan explicitly wants to go beyond simple implementation: his plan calls for closing 'repeat offender loopholes' and monitoring treatment completion, and he criticized Newsom's $100M Prop 36 budget allocation as 'a joke. It's not serious.' He is not, however, calling for further Prop 47 rollback like Bianco/Hilton, so he is short of stance 1. Quote attribution and op-ed are unusually strong primary sources.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa publicly supported Prop 36 and frames it as a drug-treatment-with-teeth measure rather than a tougher-incarceration play. He pledged in the February 2026 statewide debate to fund Prop 36 treatment as governor, putting him in the 'implement as passed' camp with a treatment-funding emphasis.
positions.source_quote: Yes, we have to fund the drug treatment in Prop. 36, and I will as governor, and yes we gotta get the guns off the street.
positions.notes: Stance 3 because he supported Prop 36 in 2024 and now commits to funding implementation, but his campaign Issues page does not have a dedicated criminal-justice section, so the primary record rests on the Feb 3 2026 KTVU debate quote. He has not advocated either further Prop 47 rollback or narrowed implementation. Confidence is medium (not high) because the source set is debate-driven rather than backed by a written campaign policy paper.

positions.summary: Thurmond is the only major Democratic candidate in the field who publicly voted against Prop 36 in 2024. He now says he will 'implement it because it's the will of the people' but would push to narrow it with more community-based substance-abuse treatment instead of jail-based programs — the closest thing to a Prop-47-friendly stance in this field.
positions.source_quote: I will implement it because it's the will of the people, [but I would make modifications, including more substance abuse treatment programs in the community because] we can't count on the jails to take care of those who have substance issues because our jails have drugs in them.
positions.notes: Stance 4 because Thurmond is the only candidate in the field who voted no on Prop 36 (concern: 'overcriminalizes' communities) and his current implementation framing explicitly leans toward narrowing the jail-mandated side in favor of community treatment. Source quote is reconstructed from KGET/KRON reporting of his governor's race interviews and the July 2024 Fox 11 debate with Bianco; the verbatim 'will of the people' phrasing was captured by multiple outlets but appears in paraphrased form in the FoxLA write-up. Reconsider stance 5 only if he ever explicitly calls for legislative rollback of Prop 36 — which, so far, he has not.

positions.summary: Hilton has called SB 54 'ridiculous' and 'unconstitutional' and pledged that as governor California 'will not have sanctuary policies of any kind.' He says his administration would be a 'clear and willing partner' with federal immigration enforcement and endorses Trump's 'worst go first' deportation framing.
positions.source_quote: It's a ridiculous policy. It's actually unconstitutional. We need to have a cooperative working relationship between the federal government and state and local government to make sure that all our laws are peacefully enforced.
