positions.source_quote: Abortion is healthcare and reproductive choice is an issue that affects all gender and sexual identities. We should not stop shouting it from the rooftops.
positions.notes: Steyer's tomsteyer.com/issues page does not have a dedicated reproductive rights section (focuses on housing, taxes, energy, AI, healthcare, ICE). Confidence medium because primary 2026-campaign-cycle reproductive-rights statement is a Facebook reaction post rather than an issues-page commitment. Coded 4 (strong defense) based on lifetime record and DSA-aligned progressive coalition; not 5 because no major expansion proposal beyond Prop 1 has been articulated.

positions.summary: Explicitly anti-abortion. Says 'life begins at conception' and 'I do not believe that an abortion is healthcare.' Would not fund Planned Parenthood as governor. Faith-driven (evangelical) conviction. Limited by Prop 1 from enacting a CA ban, but would strip state funding and end sanctuary-state policies.
positions.source_quote: I do not believe that an abortion is healthcare.
positions.notes: On KQED's Political Breakdown podcast (April 2026) Bianco said abortion is not healthcare, would defund Planned Parenthood, and on a separate occasion stated 'life begins at conception.' Stance 1 — most restrictive available; he has not proposed a specific CA gestational ban (constitutionally precluded by Prop 1), but his policy posture is to restrict by every available means (defunding, ending sanctuary cooperation).

positions.summary: Longest pro-choice public-office record in the field. As CA AG sued Trump 1.0 over abortion access and Title X gag rule; as HHS Secretary directed Planned Parenthood Title X funding to clinics. Campaign explicitly commits to expanding access. Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (April 2026).
positions.source_quote: As the husband of a high-risk Ob-Gyn, I know that abortion access is health care. … As Governor, I will ensure that California continues to lead when it comes to protecting access to abortion, to the ballot, and to live and love without restraint.
positions.notes: Coded 4 (strong defense / expand access) rather than 5 because campaign rhetoric emphasizes 'continue to lead' and protecting existing access more than a specific new constitutional amendment beyond Prop 1. Track record makes him arguably the strongest pro-choice candidate in the field; PPAC endorsement reinforces this. Could justify 5 with verbatim expansion proposal — none located by 2026-05-13.

positions.summary: Long-standing pro-choice voice; says she 'first ran for Congress to stand up for women's rights and our access to reproductive health care.' Frames reproductive rights as inseparable from women's economic equality. EMILY's List endorsed her in April 2026. Commits to keeping CA a state that 'protects and defends abortion rights.'
positions.source_quote: The attacks on abortion access and reproductive rights from extremists in Washington must end. … California must remain a state that protects and defends abortion rights and when I'm Governor we will.
positions.notes: Stance 4 — strong defense framing; no specific new constitutional amendment proposal located. Campaign issue page url confirmed live; date approximated to EMILY's List endorsement memo for verifiable cycle reference.

positions.summary: States he is pro-choice and supports taxpayer-funded abortion. As San Jose mayor has appeared with Planned Parenthood for clinic openings. Record has been criticized as inconsistent — his prior tech company stayed neutral on abortion, drawing 2022 mayoral-race criticism. No new abortion-expansion proposal in 2026 gubernatorial materials; campaign focused on housing, public safety, homelessness.
positions.source_quote: I am pro-choice and support taxpayer funded abortion, and I've never said anything to the contrary.
positions.notes: Primary on-the-record verbatim is from 2022 mayoral cycle; 2026 governor campaign site does not feature a reproductive-rights issue page. Coded 3 (hold current CA protections) rather than 4 because (a) the 2026 campaign hasn't pushed expansion rhetoric and (b) past inconsistency means there's no strong signal of leadership on expanding access. Confidence medium — could be 4 if updated 2026-cycle statements surface.

positions.summary: Pro-choice; frames reproductive freedom as economic justice. At the May 14, 2026 final debate he said he would NOT allow another state to extradite a California physician for mailing abortion pills across state lines (joining all the Democratic candidates; the two Republicans said they would). Consistent with his lifetime pro-choice record dating to the 2018 NARAL forum. 2026 campaign materials emphasize affordability, housing, and public safety with no dedicated reproductive-rights page, and he has articulated no new 2026 expansion proposals.
positions.source_quote: At the May 14, 2026 debate, asked whether they would allow Louisiana to extradite a California OB-GYN for sending abortion pills across state lines, Antonio Villaraigosa — with the other Democrats — said he would not.
positions.notes: Refreshed from a stale 2018-01-23 NARAL-forum source to the May 14, 2026 final debate, where his refusal to permit extradition of a CA abortion provider gives a current on-record datapoint. Source quote is the outlet's account of the yes/no debate question. Kept at 3: consistent pro-choice record but positioned as a more moderate Democrat with no new 2026 expansion proposals; confidence raised to high given the fresh corroboration.

positions.summary: Long pro-choice record; as State Superintendent endorsed SCA 10 (the precursor to Prop 1) to constitutionally protect abortion and contraception. As UC Regents ex-officio voted to protect comprehensive reproductive and LGBTQ-inclusive healthcare at UC facilities. As legislator and social worker says he has 'always supported measures that expand access to reproductive health care services.' Progressive lane of the 2026 field.
positions.source_quote: As a state legislator, a social worker, and now State Superintendent, I have always supported measures that expand access to reproductive health care services. At a time where we see constitutional rights being undermined at a federal level, and with the fall of Roe v. Wade now imminent, we, as Californians, must secure these rights for our state, leading the way and setting an example for the nation.
positions.notes: Verbatim quote from his 2022 CDE press release endorsing SCA 10. 2026 tonythurmond.com priorities page does not have a dedicated reproductive-rights section, but the CDE record + Regents votes + SCA 10 support are clear pro-expansion signals. Coded 4 because of the 'expand access' language and SCA 10 support; not 5 because no specific new constitutional amendment beyond Prop 1 has been proposed.

positions.summary: Strong rollback. As Day-1 governor, will issue executive order ordering every state agency to review policies for Second Amendment / Bruen compliance, direct his AG (running mate Michael Gates) to enforce uniform statewide CCW issuance, and commission legal review of CA firearm laws for unconstitutional restrictions — implicitly targeting the assault-weapons ban (Miller v. Bonta) and magazine limit (Duncan v. Bonta). Earned 'A' rating from California Rifle & Pistol Association.
positions.source_quote: I will issue an executive order directing all state agencies to review their policies, regulations, and enforcement practices to ensure they comply with the Second Amendment and recent Supreme Court rulings... direct the Attorney General to ensure every county in California complies with federal and state concealed carry law, including the standards established by the Supreme Court's decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen... conduct a comprehensive review of California's firearm laws to determine which restrictions are unconstitutional under current Supreme Court precedent.
positions.notes: Hilton's UK background does NOT moderate him on guns — his 2017 HuffPost UK piece compared post-Las-Vegas gun-control proposals to Trump's Muslim ban. The CRPA 'A' rating (March 2026) and Trump endorsement confirm full alignment with rollback wing. Source-date '2026-03-26' is approximate for the CRPA Facebook post; policy page itself has no visible publication date.

positions.summary: Strong defense of gun-safety laws. Supports assault-weapons ban, universal background checks, high-capacity-magazine ban, restrictions on ghost guns / 3D-printed / home-manufactured firearms, and a national gun license. 2026 campaign website does not feature a dedicated gun-policy page; stance is inferred from his 2019 presidential gun-violence platform, which campaign has not repudiated.
positions.source_quote: Ban high risk weapons, including assault weapons, device modifications, high capacity ammunition magazines, and strengthen laws on untraceable firearms, including ghost guns, 3D printed guns, and home manufactured guns... pass universal background checks by expanding them to private sales and unlicensed sellers and establish waiting periods at the federal level for delivery of guns... Create a national license for all gun ownership.
positions.notes: Steyer's 2026 campaign site lists 10 issue pages (housing, taxes, electricity, etc.) but no gun-policy page. Confidence is medium because 2026-specific statements are scarce; 2019 platform is most detailed primary source and remains his most-cited position. National license + new-assault-weapons ban + registry could push to 5; defaulting to 4 because he has not re-affirmed the registry idea in 2026.

positions.summary: Significant rollback. Endorsed by California Rifle & Pistol Association. As Riverside sheriff, dramatically expanded CCW issuance (from ~3,000 to >9,000 in two years) and has been the most prominent CA sheriff publicly challenging state gun laws. Celebrated 9th Circuit blocking SB 2 (sensitive-places concealed-carry restriction). Says no firearm law in California keeps people safe; favors severe penalties for criminal use rather than restrictions on lawful owners.
positions.source_quote: The Second Amendment is non negotiable. I am very proud to have the endorsement of the California Rifle and Pistol Association representing the 10 million law abiding gun owners in our beautiful state.
positions.notes: On Fox News (Jan 2024): 'he needs to drop his gun agenda, his anti-2A agenda' (re Newsom). 'I believe that every law-abiding citizen, properly-vetted, should be allowed to carry a concealed firearm if they so choose.' Has not publicly committed to non-enforcement of state assault-weapons ban as governor, but his sheriff-tenure pattern and CRPA endorsement strongly signal a stance-1 rollback orientation.

positions.summary: Strong defender of CA gun laws. As CA Attorney General (2017-2021), personally defended California's assault-weapons ban (Miller v. Becerra/Bonta) and high-capacity-magazine ban; sponsored SB 376 and AB 1669 gun-safety bills; joined 16-state AG coalition arguing 'strong, reasonable gun laws save lives' in defense of NJ magazine limits. 2026 campaign website does not yet feature a dedicated gun-policy page.
positions.source_quote: California continues to lead when it comes to implementing common-sense measures that protect our communities from gun violence.
positions.notes: Becerra's 2026 priorities (xavierbecerra2026.com) list 8 areas — gun policy is not among them — but his AG record is unambiguous and recent. Stance 4 (not 5) because the documented record is defense of *existing* laws rather than calls for major new expansions; if a campaign expansion plank emerges this could move to 5.

positions.summary: Strong defense / close loopholes. In Congress (CA-45/47), co-sponsored Assault Weapons Ban of 2022 (HR 1808) and 2023 (HR 698), and co-introduced Enhanced Background Checks Act of 2021 to close the 'Charleston loophole.' Endorsed by GIFFORDS. Supports raising firearm purchase age to 21, mandatory waiting periods, national ERPO, gun registration, and permit-to-purchase.
positions.source_quote: Congresswoman Porter is committed to advancing common sense reforms to keep families safe from gun violence. As a congresswoman, Porter co-sponsored and voted for the Bipartisan Background Checks Act and helped introduce the Enhanced Background Checks Act of 2021 to close dangerous loopholes in federal firearm laws.
positions.notes: Porter's 2026 campaign 'priorities' page lists 12 areas; gun policy is not separately featured. Stance derived from federal congressional record (assault-weapons-ban co-sponsorship, universal background checks, ERPO, registration, permit-to-purchase) — all consistent with stance 4-5. Defaulting to 4 because no 2026-specific new-expansion plank is published; would move to 5 if she publicly endorses, e.g., a state firearms registry or supply-side controls.

positions.summary: Hold-the-line moderate Democrat. Touts San Jose's 70% gun-violence reduction and frames public safety around getting *illegal* guns off streets, summer-jobs programs, and funding local LE. As San Jose councilmember in 2022 voted *against* the annual gun-owner fee (citing constitutionality and management-structure concerns) while supporting the broader liability-insurance ordinance. Backed San Jose's 'Cash for Ghost Guns' program.
positions.source_quote: San Jose is the safest big city in America, but no California community can settle for the status quo. Everyone deserves to be safe, and we'll get there by getting illegal guns off the streets, investing in summer job programs, and funding local law enforcement.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (not 4) because Mahan emphasizes enforcement-against-illegal-guns framing rather than calling for major new gun restrictions, and his vote against the SJ gun-owner fee suggests he is the most skeptical Democrat in the field toward novel regulatory schemes. He has not opposed existing CA bans. Source-date for the X post is approximate (post ID encodes Nov 2025); the X URL is the canonical primary.

positions.summary: Strong defender of gun-safety laws with a long record. As CA Assembly Speaker, co-authored and helped pass California's landmark assault-weapons ban; banned 'Saturday Night Special' cheap handguns; required safety trigger locks. As LA mayor, member of Mayors Against Illegal Guns and ran a gun-buyback program. Scored 7% from the NRA. Has publicly reaffirmed support for an assault-weapons ban.
positions.source_quote: Antonio took on the NRA to pass California's landmark assault weapons ban, banned cheap handguns that put several gun factories out of business, and required safety trigger locks on guns sold in California.
positions.notes: The campaign's own 'Record of Results' page features his gun-control work prominently — he is leaning into it as a 2026 credential, unlike some moderate Dems. Stance 4 (not 5) because the documented record is defense of and proud authorship of *existing* CA laws; no specific new-expansion 2026 plank is published. Source-date approximate (page is undated; using his 2026 campaign-launch month).

positions.summary: Strong defense; framed around school safety and removing 'weapons of war.' As State Superintendent of Public Instruction, deployed federal Mental Health First Aid Grants to schools for gun-violence prevention training and led parent-notification implementation for AB 452 / SB 906 safe-storage laws. 2026 candidate statement on the official Secretary of State voter guide explicitly names 'getting weapons of war off of our streets' as a priority.
positions.source_quote: getting weapons of war off of our streets
positions.notes: Quote is brief but explicit — 'weapons of war' is the standard Democratic shorthand for assault-style rifles and signals a 4-stance defense of CA's assault-weapons ban. Confidence medium because the campaign website itself does not include a dedicated gun-policy page; the SoS voter-guide statement is currently the most specific primary source. Source-date approximate (March 2026 voter-guide publication window).

positions.summary: Hilton opposes single-payer (cites UK experience: 'subpar patient care and taxes sky high') and wants to roll back Medi-Cal eligibility for undocumented adults, which he calls a $20B/yr line item the state can't afford. He proposes large income-tax cuts that would reduce Medi-Cal funding, with promised offsets from 'waste and fraud' enforcement. No engagement with CalCare/AB 1400 financing because he rejects the underlying program.
positions.source_quote: The actual way we deal with healthcare in this state is to at least stop spending $20 billion a year on free healthcare for illegal immigrants who shouldn't even be in the country.
positions.notes: Stance 1 (rather than 2) because Hilton explicitly campaigns on rolling back the 2024 Medi-Cal expansion to undocumented adults — that is the recent expansion this scale references. His CNN-debate analogy comparing CalCare to the UK NHS ('taxes sky high to pay for it') confirms he rejects payroll/wealth-tax financing too. Multiple debate venues and the CBS News immigrant healthcare piece corroborate.

positions.summary: Steyer is the race's most vocal single-payer champion and the only Democrat besides Porter to commit unconditionally to CalCare. He has won the California Nurses Association endorsement on this basis. On funding, he names only one concrete source: closing a corporate tax loophole worth roughly $20B/yr — orders of magnitude short of the $400-731B/yr cost estimates. Pressed for details by KFF Health News, he said 'God is going to be in the details.' He has not endorsed a payroll tax.
positions.source_quote: I will die on this hill. ... God is going to be in the details.
positions.notes: Placed at 4 rather than 5 because the only concrete revenue source he has publicly named is a corporate-tax-loophole closure (~$20B). He has explicitly NOT endorsed a payroll tax (which would put him at 5), and the CNA-backed Kalra bill (AB 1400 lineage) defers funding decisions to the Legislature. Confidence medium because he has been deliberately vague on financing — could land at 5 if he eventually accepts a payroll-tax frame, or drift toward 3 in office if no funding plan materializes. The 'God is going to be in the details' line is widely cited and a defining moment of the campaign.

positions.summary: Bianco opposes Medi-Cal coverage for undocumented immigrants ('they shouldn't be here', warns against 'incentivizing illegal entry with benefits'), and his broader platform pairs sweeping tax elimination (income tax, gas tax) with deregulation — leaving no room for a state single-payer expansion. Healthcare is not a featured issue on his campaign site; his only on-record healthcare positions are about restricting Medi-Cal eligibility.
positions.source_quote: They enter the country illegally, we're not going to incentivize them to come here to take more of the resources that regular Californians aren't getting.
positions.notes: Stance 1 with medium confidence: Bianco has not laid out a comprehensive healthcare plan on his campaign site, so this is partly inference from his immigration/Medi-Cal posture and tax-cut platform. He did soften slightly on the debate stage (recipients in asylum/residency proceedings could be covered IF they 'had to be working'), which prevents him from being a pure 1, but he otherwise frames the 2024 undocumented-adult expansion as a fiscal target. No evidence he supports any version of CalCare.

positions.summary: Becerra was a longtime single-payer advocate in Congress and as HHS Secretary, and his campaign site still says he will 'build toward a universal, single-payer CalCare system.' But after winning the California Medical Association endorsement, he materially softened: per CMA leadership, 'at this point, he wasn't supportive of single payer'; his spokesperson said 'a single payer system is the right goal — but it's not possible under this administration.' On the May 5 debate stage, when Porter directly asked whether he supports CalCare yes-or-no, he refused to answer and pivoted to Medicare for All. He names no California funding mechanism; his immediate priority is backfilling the ~$9.5B/yr Trump 'Big Beautiful Bill' cut to Medi-Cal — i.e. incremental Medi-Cal preservation, no new broad tax.
positions.source_quote: A single payer system is the right goal — but it's not possible under this administration, and right now we have a crisis on our hands.
positions.notes: Per the user's framing: 'A candidate who says I support single-payer when we can afford it but won't endorse a specific funding source is effectively stance 3.' That fits Becerra exactly post-CMA-endorsement. He knows the federal-waiver and ERISA constraints intimately ('We cannot enact in California a system of single payer' without federal law changes — LAist transcript) and frames the practical agenda as Medi-Cal cost-containment (standardizing billing codes, eliminating prior authorization), incremental coverage expansion, and reviewing the tax code for billionaire fairness — not a CalCare payroll tax. Confidence high — well documented across KQED, LAist, KFF, and the debate transcript.

positions.summary: Porter is one of two candidates (with Steyer) to commit unconditionally to delivering CalCare. Her campaign site says single-payer 'will deliver the highest quality AND most cost-effective care to the MOST people' and 'reports estimate it will save California billions in healthcare costs every year.' She argues the system needs 'a good federal partner' to be feasible. On funding she has been less specific than Steyer — her single-payer page names no specific tax — but she has separately endorsed taxing large corporations and CEO-pay-ratio measures. Her spokesperson did not respond to KFF when asked how she would actually pay for CalCare.
positions.source_quote: I have never wavered in my support for Medicare for All ... [single payer / CalCare] will deliver the highest quality AND most cost-effective care to the MOST people.
positions.notes: Placed at 4 because (a) she unconditionally commits to CalCare on her campaign site, (b) her broader tax platform leans on higher corporate taxes (not a broad payroll tax), and (c) she has not endorsed a payroll-tax frame, which would land her at 5. There is real risk she belongs at 3 given that as recently as 2025 she declined to commit on feasibility grounds, and her campaign refused KFF's funding-mechanism question — but her current public commitment to deliver CalCare and her corporate-tax lean justifies 4 over 3. Confidence medium.

positions.summary: Mahan does not support state single-payer. His healthcare platform is workforce- and access-focused: expand telehealth, allow out-of-state providers, let nurses and nurse practitioners practice at the top of their license, strengthen workforce incentives, and improve services in underserved regions. He accepts that California cannot fully backfill the Trump Medi-Cal cuts ('the magnitude of the Trump cuts is so great that we won't be able to fully do that'), implying he will manage within existing revenue rather than pursue a major new health tax. He proposes no new broad-base tax to fund healthcare.
positions.source_quote: The magnitude of the Trump cuts is so great that we won't be able to fully do that.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (incremental, no new broad tax). The Times of San Diego / KFF reporting groups him with Villaraigosa as Democrats who explicitly do not support state single-payer. His Mahan-brand 'data-driven moderate' framing and Silicon Valley donor base point away from payroll- or wealth-tax financing. No evidence he wants to roll back Medi-Cal expansion (so not 1-2). Confidence medium because his campaign has emphasized housing/homelessness/public safety over healthcare specifics, so most of this is reported positioning rather than a written healthcare plan.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa frames healthcare as a right and supports universal coverage in principle, but rejects state single-payer as fiscally and politically unrealistic — he called CalCare 'pie in the sky' on the debate stage and estimates it at ~$500B/yr requiring federal approval that won't come from the Trump administration. His Affordable California plan instead proposes a 'Golden Choice' public option through Covered California, the existing Office of Health Care Affordability for cost containment, prescription-drug cost cuts, medical-debt relief, and primary-care investment. He explicitly commits to 'hold the line on taxes' and pledges to veto 'reckless multi-billion-dollar tax hikes,' which rules out any new broad health-financing tax.
positions.source_quote: Coverage without affordability is an empty promise. ... I will hold the line on taxes and veto any reckless multi-billion-dollar tax hike on middle-class families.
positions.notes: Stance 3 (incremental + cost containment, no new broad tax). He goes meaningfully further on cost containment than a pure stance-2 candidate — public option, drug pricing, medical-debt relief — but his explicit 'hold the line on taxes' veto pledge means he cannot be placed at 4 or 5. Distinguishable from Hilton/Bianco because he does not propose rolling back the 2024 undocumented-adult Medi-Cal expansion (notes that CA already pays for ER care). Confidence high — his plan is one of the most detailed in the field.

positions.summary: Thurmond supports a state-run single-payer system to 'remove profit from healthcare' and is the only candidate in the field who has endorsed a specific NEW broad-base revenue source tied to healthcare: the California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5% tax on the ~200 California residents with a net worth over $1B, projected to raise up to $100B for health care, education, and food assistance. He has separately floated taxing assets above $150M to fund tax credits. He supports continued Medi-Cal coverage for undocumented Californians and frames healthcare in personal terms (his brother died at 35 after losing insurance). He has not endorsed a payroll tax.
positions.source_quote: No person should lose their life simply because they don't have health insurance.
positions.notes: Clean fit for stance 4: state single-payer + endorsement of a specific wealth-tax revenue mechanism (the Billionaire Tax Act), with no payroll tax. He is the only candidate in the field where the funding mechanism is concretely tied to a named ballot initiative. Note the $100B one-time revenue is still far short of the ~$400-731B/yr CalCare cost estimates — so this is best understood as the most aggressive proposed broad-base health-financing source in the field, not a complete CalCare pay-for. Confidence high — multiple independent outlets confirm the Billionaire Tax Act endorsement.

positions.summary: Hilton's published education plan calls for expanding choice through Education Savings Accounts (starting with low-income and special-needs students), cross-district open enrollment regardless of zip code, and a parent-trigger mechanism that converts D-graded schools to charter models after two years. His running mate Gloria Romero is an explicit voucher advocate.
positions.source_quote: To give parents immediate options while traditional schools improve, Hilton will expand choice through ESAs, starting with low-income and special needs students... parents will be free to move their children to any public school that performs better, regardless of zip code... If a school receives a D grade two years in a row, parents will have the right to trigger administrative changes, curriculum overhauls, or conversion to a charter model.
positions.notes: Stance 1 fits: ESAs for low-income/special-needs students are functionally vouchers in everything but name, and the parent-trigger-to-charter mechanism is the most aggressive charter-expansion lever currently used anywhere in the country. He stops short of universal vouchers (Bianco's territory) — but his ticket explicitly includes a voucher advocate (Romero), so the overall package is unambiguously at the maximum-expansion end of the California Overton window.

positions.summary: Steyer's education platform is built around investing tax revenue into public schools (he proposes ~$50B/year in new revenue) and making education free from preschool through community college. He has publicly said he does not support using public money for private or religious education. The California Teachers Association endorsed him in April 2026 specifically over the charter-skeptical Thurmond.
positions.source_quote: Make corporations pay their fair share, and put that money into our public schools to make California a top ten state for education... I'm enormously proud to have the endorsement of @WeAreCTA.
positions.notes: Stance 5 (cap/freeze charters, redirect to public schools) is supported by (a) the CTA endorsement, which is the single strongest signal a CA Democrat is fully aligned with the union-side charter posture; (b) Steyer's 2020 stated opposition to public money for private education; (c) his education platform listing zero charter-supportive policies and treating public-school investment as the entire answer. He has not personally called for a charter cap, so the position-specifically-on-charters confidence is technically medium — but the CTA's endorsement effectively commits him to that coalition, hence overall high confidence.

positions.summary: Bianco is the most aggressive school-choice candidate in the field. At the December 2025 California School Boards Association forum he was the only candidate to publicly back universal vouchers, comparing the choice to picking 'the restaurant with the best food.' His campaign platform pairs this with expanded high-performing charters.
positions.source_quote: If you are deciding where you want to eat dinner, you choose the restaurant with the best food, and the other restaurant is not going to get your service until they change their policies. I will be the only person offering voucher systems for all of your kids... Encourage and expand access to high-performing charter schools that are creating innovative new learning environments outside of our public-school districts.
positions.notes: Stance 1 — universal vouchers PLUS charter expansion is the maximum school-choice position available; he is to Hilton's right on this axis because Hilton's ESAs start narrow (low-income/special-needs) while Bianco proposes universal.

positions.summary: Becerra's 2026 campaign is silent on K-12 charters and vouchers — education is not among his 8 listed priorities. However his record as California AG (2017-2021) places him on the regulation/skeptic side: he issued a 2018 advisory opinion subjecting charter schools to the Brown Act and Public Records Act (more oversight), and led a multistate lawsuit against Secretary DeVos blocking diversion of pandemic relief funds to private schools.
positions.source_quote: Again, and again, the Trump Administration takes action to steal from the poor and give to the rich. Congress set clear parameters on how to spend this money in order to confront the devastating effects of a pandemic on our schools.
positions.notes: Coded 4 (lean toward more oversight, no vouchers) based on AG record, not 2026 campaign statements. His 2018 AG advisory subjecting charters to Brown Act / Public Records Act is widely read as part of the regulation-of-charters wave that produced AB 1505 in California; it is a transparency/oversight stance rather than an explicit cap. His DeVos lawsuit on pandemic funds is unambiguously anti-voucher-style diversion. Could plausibly be coded 3 if reviewer prefers to anchor only to 2026 silence; coded 4 here because the AG record is the only substantive evidence and it points one direction. Confidence is LOW because his 2026 campaign has said nothing about K-12 charters specifically and AG actions on transparency are not the same as opposing charters.

positions.summary: Porter's 2026 campaign issue page is silent on K-12 charters specifically, but her documented record is firmly anti-voucher and pro-traditional-public-school. She opposed the 2018 Christian Coalition voucher question, has publicly attacked Betsy DeVos's school-choice agenda, and as House Oversight ranking member framed the fix for K-12 as fully funding public schools and paying teachers a living wage rather than alternatives.
positions.source_quote: Education Vouchers that Allow Parents to Choose a Public or Private School for their Children. (Opposes)
positions.notes: Coded 4 not 5 because she has no on-record statement calling for a cap or reduction in California charter authorizations; her position is best read as 'oppose vouchers, fund public schools fully' rather than 'shut down charters.' The verbatim primary source quote is from a Christian Coalition voter-guide survey response. The isidewith aggregator records her vouchers position as 'No, we should focus on improving our public schools instead' — same direction. Her 2026 governor priorities page lists only tuition-free college and free childcare; she does not discuss K-12 at all, which is the main sourcing gap.

positions.summary: Mahan's 2026 education platform is built entirely around accountability inside the traditional public-school system — science of reading, high-dosage tutoring, performance-based teacher rewards, unifying the State Board of Education with the Department of Education — and is silent on charter schools, vouchers, and ESAs. As San Jose mayor he has no public charter-authorization record (school districts in San Jose are independent of city government). The absence of any pro-voucher or pro-charter-expansion statement, combined with his framing as a public-school-reform Democrat rather than a school-choice Democrat, supports a neutral stance.
positions.source_quote: Implement science of reading and other evidence-based curricular and pedagogical practices. Fund high-dosage tutoring programs that train college students to tutor elementary school children who fall behind in reading and math with an emphasis on 3rd grade reading levels. Reward teachers whose students outperform peer cohorts and mandate coaching/training for teachers whose students consistently underperform peer cohorts.
positions.notes: Coded 3 (neutral on charters, no voucher support) with LOW confidence. Mahan is the most education-engaged of the three (former TFA middle-school English/history teacher; wife runs a high school serving first-gen low-income students) and has the most detailed K-12 platform — yet that platform completely omits charters and vouchers, which is unusual for a tech-moderate Democrat. Reasonable readings could place him at 2 (sympathetic to charters as part of accountability/choice agenda, given his outcomes-focused framing and Silicon Valley tech-donor base) or 3 (genuinely neutral). With no direct quote either way, 3 is the conservative choice. As San Jose mayor he has no charter-authorization vote on record because California city mayors do not authorize charters — school districts and county boards of education do. Date estimated (GrowSF questionnaire window). The San Jose Spotlight piece criticizing Mahan for school closures explicitly notes the mayor lacks legal authority over school board decisions, which is why no charter-renewal record exists for him to cite.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa is the field's most prominent pro-charter Democrat by long-form record: as Assembly Speaker in 1998 he brokered the deal that lifted California's charter cap, as LA Mayor he championed charter expansion, and his 2018 gubernatorial run drew $22M+ in independent expenditures from CCSA, Bloomberg, Hastings, Broad, Walton, and Oberndorf. He told EdSource in 2018 he supports 'quality charters and quality traditional public schools' but opposes for-profit charters. His 2026 platform is silent on K-12.
positions.source_quote: I believe in unions... I'm for great schools, whether they are charter or traditional... But we are living at a time when somehow you are anti-union because you stand up and say 'Hey, I want to put the kids first.'
positions.notes: Stance 2 (expand charters, protect parental choice) is the long-form record. Confidence is medium rather than high because (a) his 2026 platform deliberately omits K-12, suggesting he may be triangulating away from the 2018 CCSA-funded image in a CTA-dominated Democratic primary; (b) he has also said he opposes for-profit charters and wants accountability, which is a step softer than stance 1. Worth re-coding if he publishes a 2026 K-12 plank or stakes out a clearer position in debate.

positions.summary: Thurmond is the field's most identifiably charter-skeptical candidate by governing record: he beat charter advocate Marshall Tuck in 2018 with $8M in CTA backing, then as Superintendent convened the statewide Charter School Task Force whose recommendations became AB 1505 (2019) — the law giving districts more authority to deny charter petitions on fiscal-impact grounds. He publicly thanked Newsom and the legislature on signing day. His 2026 platform leads with a five-year third-grade literacy plan and a shift from ADA to enrollment-based funding (a pro-traditional-public-schools structural reform).
positions.source_quote: I want to thank Governor Newsom, Assemblymember O'Donnell, and all the stakeholders for this important legislation [AB 1505]... [The bill] empowering communities to consider the fiscal impact of new charter schools on existing schools in the neighborhood, increasing accountability and transparency for all charter schools.
positions.notes: Stance 4 (restrict charter expansion) rather than 5 (cap/freeze): AB 1505 deliberately did not impose a charter cap — it gave districts more denial authority and fiscal-impact discretion, which is the policy stance Thurmond championed. The shift from ADA to enrollment-based funding also reinforces this — it directly addresses the funding pressure traditional districts face when charters draw students away. Notably, CTA's 2026 gubernatorial endorsement went to Steyer, not Thurmond, possibly because Steyer's stance 5 framing is even more union-aligned and because Thurmond is polling far back. Thurmond's stance is well-documented even though charters have not been a centerpiece of his 2026 campaign messaging.

positions.summary: Hilton argues California already spends more than $22,000 per student and that outcomes are a leadership and accountability problem, not a funding problem. His K-12 plan explicitly does not require more spending; he would instead expand school choice through Education Savings Accounts (starting with low-income and special needs students), grade every school and teacher, weaken tenure (5-year minimum), and let parents trigger charter conversion of failing schools.
positions.source_quote: California spends more than $22,000 per student each year, among the highest in the nation, yet outcomes continue to decline. This is not a funding problem. It is a leadership and accountability problem... This approach does not require more spending. It requires a new focus on results.
positions.notes: Stance 2 (hold or modestly trim) is the best fit: he is not promising literal cuts to Prop 98, but he explicitly says no new money is needed, wants ESAs (which divert dollars from district schools), and the EdSource/Local News Matters debate writeup bucketed him with Bianco as Republicans who 'say schools don't need more funding and should cut wasteful spending.' If he leaned into ESAs aggressively this could move to stance 1, but the published plan stops short of net cuts.

positions.summary: Steyer would raise up to $50 billion in new revenue by closing corporate tax loopholes (including a commercial Prop 13 split-roll reform) and taxing wealthy individuals, splitting it between health care and education. He pairs that with explicit teacher-pay increases for recruitment and retention, universal free school meals year-round, and pre-K starting at age 3 — and notes California ranks 31st in the nation in per-pupil funding adjusted for cost of living.
positions.source_quote: Steyer has proposed investing more money in public schools and increasing teacher pay to help recruit and retain them... He says he'll generate up to $50 billion in new revenue by raising taxes on corporations and wealthy individuals, with funds split between health care and education.
positions.notes: Stance 5 (major new funding via dedicated tax) is the cleanest fit because Steyer ties new K-12 dollars to a specific revenue mechanism (corporate loophole closure, Trump-loophole closure, commercial Prop 13 reform). CTA endorsement reinforces alignment with teacher-pay increases.

positions.summary: Bianco argues California already spends more on education than any other state with the lowest results, so the answer is redirecting dollars (to teachers, classrooms, training, recruitment, career-technical education, and charter schools), not adding more. He wants school funding to go 'directly to teachers, students, and the classroom' and rolls in a school-resource-officer mandate and repeal of AB 1955.
positions.source_quote: California spends more on education than any other state, and yet we see some of the lowest metrics of success and student learning... Ensure school funding goes directly to teachers, students, and the classroom.
positions.notes: Stance 2: he does not call for outright cuts, but he is explicit that no new K-12 dollars are needed and frames current spending as wasteful. He does say increase 'funding for teacher training and recruitment programs' specifically, which keeps him from a 1; this is targeted reallocation, not net new investment.

positions.summary: Becerra has not published a K-12 funding position. His 2026 priorities page lists eight issue areas (health care, fighting Trump, housing, economy & affordability, energy & utilities, disaster preparedness, AI, homelessness) with no education section, and EdSource's April 30, 2026 candidate-by-candidate education-funding comparison attributed no quote or position to him on K-12 funding — an omission a commenter on the article called 'inexcusable.' He may align with the broader Democratic field's pro-funding posture, but he has offered no specific Prop 98, LCFF, teacher-pay, or school-bond commitment that would place him on the 1–5 scale.
positions.source_quote: No mention of Xavier Becerra's stances on improving education, but you include the ones from candidates polling in single digits? That's inexcusable.
positions.notes: The source_quote above is a reader-comment observation on the EdSource article, not a Becerra statement — used because the verifiable, citable fact here is the documented absence of a Becerra position in the most comprehensive 2026 K-12 funding comparison piece. Primary sources searched and confirmed silent on K-12: (1) https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/priorities/ — eight issue pages, none on education; (2) https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/bio/ — no K-12 mention; (3) https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/governor/ — lists only climate goals and a utility/insurance-rate freeze as Becerra priorities; (4) https://laist.com/news/politics/2026-election-california-primary-xavier-becerra-california-governor-transcript — Larry Mantle interview covers healthcare, budget, homelessness, gas, immigration, labor, pandemic preparedness, with zero mention of K-12, schools, teachers, Prop 98, LCFF, or school bonds; (5) EdSource's comparison article names Becerra as a top candidate but attributes no K-12 quote or position to him; (6) Local News Matters republication confirms same null result. iSideWith lists charter / voucher / book-ban positions for Becerra but explicitly attributes them to 'voterbase' inference and 'ChatGPT Party Research,' not primary sources, so they are not citable. The California Faculty Association co-endorsement with Thurmond is about higher education / CFA faculty, not K-12. Federal congressional voting on Title I-style funding (1993–2017) did not surface specific evidence in searches and would in any case not directly resolve a California Prop 98 / LCFF stance. Honest finding: insufficient data.

positions.summary: Porter's published campaign priorities center on tuition-free public universities (paid for by closing corporate tax loopholes / raising corporate taxes) and childcare, not on a specific K-12 dollar number. EdSource grouped her with Democrats who support increased K-12 funding through corporate taxes, but she has not published a Prop 98-scale or dedicated-bond K-12 plan as Steyer and Thurmond have.
positions.source_quote: Porter: tuition-free state universities for California residents by raising corporate taxes... Democratic candidates largely agree that schools need more funding while Republicans disagree.
positions.notes: Stance 4 (modest increases) is the best fit given (a) the Democratic baseline she shares per EdSource, (b) her teacher background and Warren-style consumer-protection framing, and (c) the absence of a dedicated K-12 tax/bond proposal that would justify stance 5. If she publishes a K-12 plan with a specific revenue source, revisit.

positions.summary: Mahan, a former Teach for America middle-school teacher, frames K-12 as a 'five-alarm fire' on test scores and would invest in high-dosage tutoring, evidence-based phonics literacy curricula, and performance-linked teacher rewards/coaching. As a moderate Democrat he opposes new broad-based taxes and emphasizes accountability and outcomes over raw spending levels; his vision references using existing tax revenue for schools and a 'shared prosperity fund.'
positions.source_quote: As governor, I would set clear goals for literacy—closing racial gaps and getting all students reading at grade level—because reading proficiency opens doors to opportunity... Evidence-based instruction like phonics improves literacy. Tracking student progress and providing targeted tutoring when students fall behind works.
positions.notes: Stance 4 reflects: targeted new investment (tutoring, literacy coaching) without a dedicated new revenue mechanism. He is more skeptical of net new state K-12 spending than Steyer/Thurmond and more interested in performance-pay reform than the CTA-aligned Democrats. Could arguably be stance 3 if you weight the no-new-taxes posture heavily; I picked 4 because his published proposals (high-dosage tutoring at scale, evidence-based curricula adoption with district accountability) cost real money.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa positions himself as the 'education governor,' citing his Assembly Speaker record of 'record investments in public schools,' significantly increased per-pupil funding, class-size reduction, and a 'historic bipartisan school bond' to repair and build schools — plus the LAUSD turnaround. On the 2026 trail his focus is outcomes and dual enrollment / career-technical education rather than a new dedicated tax, and he stresses California is 'No. 1 in teacher pay' but '21st in per-pupil spending' and 'dead last in graduation.'
positions.source_quote: Made record investments in public schools, including the largest single allocation of school safety funds in state history... Significantly increased per pupil funding in public schools... Passed historic bipartisan school bond to repair old schools and build new schools.
positions.notes: Stance 4 reflects modest funding increases (especially facilities via bonds, dual enrollment, career-tech) without a Steyer-scale dedicated tax mechanism. Most of his public language is about doing more with current dollars and closing achievement gaps; he is the candidate most likely to revive a school facilities bond. If he publishes a billionaire-tax-for-schools proposal, revisit toward 5.

positions.summary: As the sitting Superintendent of Public Instruction, Thurmond has the most developed K-12 funding posture: he criticized Newsom's 2026-27 budget as 'falling short of funding levels and meaningful reforms needed to truly accelerate student achievement,' opposed Newsom's plan to shift TK-12 governance away from his elected office, called out California's reliance on average daily attendance for school revenue, and is running on closing tax loopholes and taxing billionaires (he endorses the California Billionaire Tax Act / a tax on residents with >$150M in assets) to fund education. He is also pushing a $10B affordable-housing bond aimed partly at educator/public-worker housing on surplus school land, and a five-year 'Literacy Moonshot.'
positions.source_quote: [The budget proposal] falls short of funding levels and meaningful reforms needed to truly accelerate student achievement... [The governance proposal] shifts authority to implement TK-12 education programs away from the official who California voters have elected to lead our state's public schools.
positions.notes: Stance 5 (major new funding via dedicated tax or bond) is unambiguous: Thurmond is publicly tying K-14 funding to a billionaire wealth tax, has an active state-superintendent record of pushing for more than the Governor proposed, and explicitly opposes shifting K-12 governance authority out of the elected SPI office. He is also the most LCFF-fluent voice in the field and the most likely to push for an ADA-to-enrollment funding-base shift.

positions.summary: Would replace California's 13.3% graduated top marginal income-tax rate with a flat 7.5% rate on income above $100,000 — a large cut for top earners — and eliminate the $800 minimum LLC tax. No corporate-rate increase.
positions.source_quote: California has built the highest and most punitive state income tax system in America, with top rates reaching 13.3 percent. ... A single, simple 7.5% rate on income above $100,000. ... No state income tax on your first $100,000.

positions.summary: Steyer's revenue plan does NOT raise the 13.3% personal income rate or the 8.84% statutory corporate rate. It is structural: closing the 'water's edge' corporate loophole, a split-roll commercial property tax, and backing a special 2027 election in his first year as governor to raise corporate (commercial property) taxes — together with the billionaire wealth tax — to raise ~$20B/year. Because he raises the effective burden on corporations and the wealthy via loopholes and property-tax reform rather than statutory rate hikes, this is a modest rate-direction increase (3), not a substantial bracket/rate raise (4).
positions.source_quote: I am proposing closing a corporate real estate tax loophole that's existed for over 40 years. That brings in more money to the state, that is permanent, that is completely fair.

positions.summary: Signature pledge to eliminate California's state income tax entirely — including the top bracket — funded by spending cuts, anti-fraud enforcement, and expanded oil drilling. No corporate-rate increase.
positions.source_quote: You eliminate all of the fraud, you become oil independent and use that to fund government, and now we don't have to pay income taxes.

positions.summary: Says he would raise effective tax rates on wealthy Californians whose passive (capital-gains) income is taxed below what teachers, nurses, and firefighters pay on wages. At the May 14, 2026 final debate, pressed on how he would fund his agenda, he named a specific mechanism for the first time: restricting some corporations' use of tax credits (mirroring Newsom's same-day budget proposal). Still has not endorsed a top-bracket or general corporate-rate change; framing remains directional ('they'll pay more').
positions.source_quote: We will make sure that those who have really large wealth, if they are paying less than a teacher or a firefighter or a police officer or a nurse, that they're going to be paying more in taxes. ... All that passive income — capital gains and other types of income — is taxed far differently.
positions.notes: Stance unchanged at 3. May 14, 2026 final debate added specificity (restrict corporate tax-credit use, per CalMatters/KPBS) but not a rate change, so still 'make the wealthy/corporations pay more' without a bracket move. Primary quote retained from the SF Examiner profile; debate sources added as secondary corroboration.

positions.summary: Centerpiece is a 'Progressive Corporate Tax' replacing the flat 8.84% corporate rate with a graduated scale topping out around 9.75% for the largest, most profitable corporations (~$8B/year), paired with eliminating state income tax under $100K. A modest corporate-rate increase on top earners, not a substantial broad raise.
positions.source_quote: As Governor, I will launch a Progressive Corporate Tax. ... Even less than a one percent increase on the most profitable businesses earning hundreds of millions in profit will generate up to $8 billion in annual revenue.

positions.summary: Opposes broad tax increases, says 'raising taxes isn't always the answer,' and commits to not raising broad-based taxes to fix the budget. Lone exception is a narrow sectoral levy on AI: his May 2026 'hold Big Tech accountable' plan formalizes a 'Shared Prosperity Fund' directing a portion of tax revenue from data centers and robotics manufacturers into job-training and apprenticeship programs (he floated UBI only 'if we see mass job loss'). Not a top-bracket or general corporate-rate increase; proposes no rate cuts either, so holds current rates.
positions.source_quote: Raising taxes isn't always the answer, Tom.
positions.notes: Stance unchanged at 2. The May 14-15, 2026 tech-accountability plan formalized the previously vague 'narrow sectoral tax on AI companies' into a named 'Shared Prosperity Fund' financed by data-center/robotics tax revenue. Primary quote retained; SF Standard added as secondary.

positions.summary: Would make the 13.3% top rate permanent only conditional on a spending plan, and opposes new state-level hikes ('we can't tax our way out of our problems'). Says billionaires should pay more but that it's a federal job. Proposes no cuts and no state rate increase — holds current rates.
positions.source_quote: With respect to making permanent the 13%, which is the highest upper-income tax in the United States, I think we should do it, but not unless we do a spending plan.

positions.summary: Thurmond's articulated tax program is the billionaire wealth tax plus a tax credit for working- and middle-class families. No source reviewed (KQED, LAist, CalMatters, KPBS, official voter guide) articulates a position on the personal income-tax RATE (13.3%) or the corporate-tax RATE (8.84%) distinct from the wealth tax. Per sourcing rules, his income/corporate RATE direction is not coded and is NOT inferred from his wealth-tax support.
Opposes a state wealth tax; frames California as having 'a spending problem, not a revenue problem' and opposes Prop 13 changes. His plan cuts taxes rather than adding a net-worth levy.
positions.source_quote: California has built the highest and most punitive state income tax system in America, with top rates reaching 13.3 percent.

positions.summary: Steyer — himself a billionaire — has said he would vote for the November 2026 billionaire wealth-tax initiative and frames his campaign around taxing the wealthy and corporations to fund health care, education, and care work.
positions.source_quote: If there's an opportunity to tax wealthy people to fund health care and education, I'd vote for it all day long.

positions.summary: Opposes any new state tax; his signature pledge is to eliminate the state income tax entirely. A net-worth/wealth tax is contrary to his whole platform.
positions.source_quote: You eliminate all of the fraud, you become oil independent and use that to fund government, and now we don't have to pay income taxes.

positions.summary: Opposes the one-time billionaire wealth-tax initiative on stability grounds — argues California needs predictable, recurring revenue rather than a one-time levy — while saying wealthy Californians should pay more (targeting passive/capital-gains income). Skeptical of the wealth-tax mechanism but wants the wealthy to pay more, so coded 2 (skeptical, no current support) rather than outright 1.
positions.source_quote: Most of the government's revenue is income tax ... we're only taxing those who get paid by check, by salary. And all that passive income — capital gains and other types of income — is taxed far differently.

positions.summary: Now on record: at the May 2026 gubernatorial debate Porter opposed Tom Steyer's proposed one-time billionaire wealth-tax initiative, calling it 'too narrow' and saying it 'wouldn't make a real change.' Her own platform centers on a graduated corporate tax and cutting income tax under $100K rather than a net-worth levy. Like Becerra, she criticizes this specific mechanism as insufficient while still favoring making the wealthy and corporations pay more — a skeptical 'no current support' posture rather than principled anti-tax opposition.
positions.source_quote: Porter, meanwhile, said the tax was too narrow and wouldn't make a real change.
positions.notes: Recoded from unknown to 2 after the May 5-6, 2026 CNN/ABC7 debate put her on record against Steyer's one-time billionaire tax ('too narrow', 'wouldn't make a real change'). Coded 2 (lean against / no current support) rather than 1, mirroring Becerra: her critique is from the left (the mechanism is insufficient) and she still wants the wealthy/corporations to pay more via a graduated corporate tax. Confidence medium — clear single on-record debate line; she has not addressed a recurring state wealth tax in principle.

positions.summary: Explicitly opposes the one-time billionaire wealth-tax initiative, alongside his broader commitment to not raising broad-based taxes to fix budget holes.
positions.source_quote: [Mahan] has committed to not raising taxes to fix budget holes — including with a one-time tax on billionaires that most of his rivals are also against.

positions.summary: Opposes the billionaire wealth-tax initiative; says billionaires should pay more but that it is the federal government's job, warning that wealthy Californians 'are leaving as we speak.' Pledges to veto reckless multi-billion-dollar state tax hikes.
positions.source_quote: What I've said is billionaires should pay more than the rest of us, but the federal government should do that because at, at the end of the day, they're just leaving and they're leaving as we speak.

positions.summary: Thurmond is the only major Democratic candidate besides Steyer who openly supports the November 2026 one-time 5% billionaire wealth-tax initiative, framing it as the way to fund schools, health care, and food assistance, paired with a tax credit for working/middle-class families.
positions.source_quote: My proposal is to tax billionaires in our state and then use that revenue for our needs. And, to give a tax credit to working people, middle-class people, so they have more money in their pocket every month to pay for the rising cost of gas, groceries, and housing.
